notes.title: Masi Maham Theerthavari
body: There were two ways to go that morning. One pointed right—to the ERC Voices conference taking place at Pondicherry’s École française d'Extrême-Orient (EFEO). One pointed left—to the location of the Masi Maagam Kadal Theerthavari on the beachfronts of Vaithikuppam, which is where the fisher communities of Pondicherry have long-lived.

This is one of three great gatherings that happens on this town’s coastal line (the other two are Aadi amavasya and Thai amavasya) but this one falls on pournami, the night of the full moon. The festival gets its name from the coincidence of the full moon (or its closeness) with Maha nakshatram. The Maham of the month of Masi, the great Maham or Mahamaham, or masi magam as it is colloquially known is the largest and most significant of the three for this reason and because it draws deities from elsewhere too: Senji Ranganathaswamy, Malayanoor Angalamman, Mailam Murugan.

Crowds are a hindrance to those who do not participate in this town’s temple traditions, and a draw to those who do because the day offers so many darshans in a single place. To my mind, there was no real choice. I had to go not where Pondicherry’s ritual life was being studied and theorised, but where it was being so richly and elaborately lived. The crowds around me pulled; all I needed to do was to move with them. So, I did.

Manish Maheshwari and Inbar Maor were in town and joined me. We followed the paths of the deities who were still beachside (many had come early and left already). We haggled with hawkers peddling their wares on spread-out cloth, speaking strange mixtures of Hindi and Tamil. We watched a Nataraja dancing in the waves–from which temple, we couldn’t tell (the videos of this you see are taken by Inbar Maor). Tillai vananathar, one man said, but that wasn’t precise enough. We got stuck in the crowds. We didn’t stop for annadanam which was being given out in one of the small roads adjoining. Manish shaded himself with a copy of Nick Dirks’ Castes of Mind which he happened to have on hand, and which I found hilarious. We each had our moorings and our leanings but this wasn’t the place for them. We spoke about all things Masi Maagam, and nothing about a project or a plan to document Pondicherry’s temples. All that came before, or after, I don’t precisely recall.

But “Sthalam” as we know it now started there, that precise coincidence of pournami with maha nakshatram, in those waters, in that effervescent mix of heady crowd, hot sun, and the crowd of Gods come to bathe in the purifying waters of the place we know as Pondicherry.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil: First Visit and Pradosham
body: We’ve decided, thanks largely to Debbie Wastie being in town with her camera, to go to the Chetty Koyil. Debbie is here to help me photograph Pondicherry’s culinary traditions, which are too often reduced to a Frenchness which truly doesn’t exist here any more, if it ever did at all. But I’m also in search of temple food, food in temples–and what food means in the context of ritual worship, which is a whole other thing (eg: what does it mean for the deity to eat? Why do we place so many edibles on the body of God? What does it mean to feed the hungry fire? What exactly is prasadam? And so on). So Ganesan Sir has requested permission from the Chetty Koyil on Mission Street which have kindly been granted, that morning he makes introductions, and so we get started with a full walk around the prakaram to get a full set of descriptive notes.

That evening, Debbie and I return for Pradosham. Sivan, Ambal, and the Vrushabha in his mandapam get full abhishekams. Following this, Pradosha Nayaka and his consort are hoisted onto a silver vrushabha, and taken thrice around the prakaram: a classic ul-purappadu or inside procession. The place gets quite crowded. Many women push the cart holding the processional forms, but there is no singing or recitation during the purappadu. After the final deeparadhanai, everyone sits quietly in two lines facing each other, to await prasadam. This is quite sumptuous: panchamritam, puttu, kesari, puli-saadam.

All photographs of that day are Debbie’s, kindly shared, though they are a mixed documentation: preparations for pradosham (all the materials needed for all 3 abhishekams were grouped and kept ready ahead of time) and for the Brahmotsavam coming soon (the yagasala being cleared of all the saris and fabrics stored there). That upcoming event presents naturally as the next thing for which to return. It becomes the Sthalam’s first major ritual immersion.

notes.title: Manimutthumariamman Koyil, Friday Abhishekam
body: I arrive at this temple thanks to Ramanan Gurukkal who tends to the small Pillaiyar in our old building (and goes in the evenings to the Murugan temple in Lawspet–almost an indication that we should go there, too). I want to ask about food, but it appears that the path to food is through ritual and so I submit to that instead, and attend the regular Friday abhishekam that happens here around noon. The temple is a theruvu koyil, a streetside shrine, but it has a sthala vriksha at the back (neem and peepul, bound together), which you access through the tiniest of prakarams. There is a small amman under the tree. Manimutthumariamman is seated here, her full-figured form (not just the head, as elsewhere). There is a lady I will come to know as Kasturi mami, who comes to help prepare the alankarams, draw kolam etc. She does the ubhayam for this ritual, out of gratitude to the Goddess for helping her find food one day at the temple when she needed it (the temple does a regular Annadanam also on Fridays). Now she makes sure that the temple has what it needs to continue this practice, whether she’s around or not.

Abhishekam is a simple but complete affair, a crowd slowly gathers. I meet a man who heads a group for Sivaratri preparations at the Veapuriswara Koyil; he promises to help me make introductions there later. The Nirvagam head is around, too, and very helpful. After the event is over and prasadam and food (which arrives in a truck in a large patram) is distributed (many bring dabbas to carry away–I sit and talk to Ramanan Gurukkal about the temple and its practices. Its major festival is in Aadi masam. Otherwise it is a 1-kalam puja temple, with these Friday abhishekams being the main recurrent practice.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil Brahmotsavam Preparatory Pujas
body: We have missed an early morning Manakkula Vinayaka Abhishekam (the Chetty Koyil maintains certain formal, ritual relations with that other important Pondicherry shrine) and a puja at the Lada Chinnamman Koyil (which is the temple’s Amman shrine and kulam – called Keni Kulam – all this is a distance away near the Ramakrishna School on Lally Tollendal/ Iswaran Koyil Street).

That evening was the Anugnai (seeking sanction, consent, and blessing), the temple’s own Vigneswara Puja. I believe there’s a Vinayaka purappadu, which goes to Keni kulam, next to the Lada Chinnamman koyil, where the Mrtsangrahanam or the collection of sacred earth happens (Keni Kulam mann eduthal, the patrikai says).
Where does the Vastu shanti puja happen? The ankurarpanam or seed-sprouting? Need to make sure we attend this festival next year to be sure.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil Brahmotsavam Day 1 Dhvajarohanam
body: The day of the Dhvajarohanam, Kodi Yettral or flag raising, marks the formal beginning of the Brahmotsavam itself. The little astra murti–the one that eventually takes a dip in the sea on the Theerthavari day–is kept on a stool to the left of the dhvajastambha, and all archanais and offerings are made to it as well. All other utsava murtis are out, watching the bali offerings and the deeparadhnais. The officiating priest, Venkatesa Gurukkal, directs the mangala vadyam ragas–Shankarabharanam, Sri Ragam etc. He remarks later that this could have gone on for hours, but the event had started late and that required dynamic alterations to keep within the time marked for the flag raising. Shankaranaryana Chettiar carries the kodi around the temple, and then it goes up.

It’s Arunaditya’s first day with Sthalam as a project, and we are both very visible with our cameras. Already we are being asked for photos; this is the beginning of a period when our phone contacts will start to grow and names will now be classified based on at which temple we met anyone. A young girl named Manounemani asks for photos and spells her name so we get it right because of its French inflections. She tells us her father was fond of the Manonmani amman nearby so she is named after the Goddess. Indeed, there is a small Maonmani Amman theruvu koyil nearby. We take this as direction to include that small shrine in our list of temples to document.

notes.title: Angalamman Koyil Vallala Kottai
body: Evening, Angalamman. Intense! Outside the Angalamman temple in Angalanagar (Muthialpet, in its larger placement) is a ground on which a massive figure of Vallalaraja’s queen Villalasini or Vallala Kandi as she is called has been shaped in mud and decorated with coloured powders. Her hair is spread wide, almost a halo, and strewn with flower garlands–marigolds, tellingly, which are never used in pujas partly because they are not a native flower, but not just marigolds. She is carrying a child who is Siva (thanks to a boon granted to Vallalaraja in recognition of his penances) and can be born in two forms. If he is born at the right moment and does not touch the ground, his force as a manifestation of Siva will be unstoppable, the cosmos stands to be destabilized. If he does touch the ground, however, it is prophesied (somehow) that the power of his birth will be transferred away from Vallalaraja, and will cause his death and the destruction of his line. Just now the pregnant wife is lying in the ground, birth is imminent. We all know what must happen, but just how is where all the magic of this evening lies.

Meantime, camphor lamps are lit and incense and kunkuma offered to the prone figure of the Queen, who is carrying the Siva yet to be born, after all. Policemen are everywhere. This event has, in the past, caused conflict between different Angalamman-worshipping communities in the region, each claiming Her for their own and the rights to conduct the festival in her honour, too. In fact, there’s an Angalamman temple being built on the beach side of the sudukaadu or graveyard nearby, and that one belongs to the fishermen. Our temple as we understand is a Vanniar-Gounder-Padayatchi shrine. Not sure which community keeps control of the Angalamman Koyil in Pondicherry’s main town area; that’s the other significant one in this region.

The story of the evening is being told by Senthil Pusari, who comes from a family of hereditary pambaikaras, aided by a sidekick who throws up errors while listening that make for good amusement. A green-faced thirunangai joins the group, after a while. Is she the fortune-teller who becomes the mid-wife who is Periyachi or Pecchayiamman? Dressed in a strange light-suit with a tall, triangular head-dress topped with a disc and fitted with lights, out comes Vallalaraja himself. A host of “swamis” (as people call them) follow: thirunangais dressed as terrible goddesses, and other heavily painted figures we cannot recognize.

Vallalaraja has a grand welcoming into the ground (but is immediately made to halt temporarily due to some serial lights malfunctioning!!). Vallalaraja and the green Thirunangai take countless rounds conversing, arguing, mocking, threatening, justifying, re-questioning, rebutting, and also at one point, kicking!
All this goes on for long, as crowds gather.

Two deities emerge from the temple, eventually. They go around the temple prakaram once, and then emerge into the road, the processional and dramatic storytelling space, where their carriages and vahanas wait. One is clearly Angalamman, standing in a warrior stance, legs wide apart. The other is Pecchayiamman, here the mid-wife (maruthuvachi) who births Siva, the body of the Queen laid across her lap so that the birth does not happen on the ground – she has the Queen’s body torn, the infant child held high up by her right hand, and entrails garlanding everything. But she emerges with a long black cloth covering her. This cloth comes onto the ground and encircles the prone Queen figure–presumably, this is the now the scene of birthing.

Amman is clearly loaded on a vahana vandi going East, but we lose track of her. Her veethi ula perhaps takes a long route returning only much later in the night. We presume her path marks out the area which is the Kottai (fort) or is the fort encirclement (Kottai Valam), to commemorate her victory over the demon king.

Pecchayiamman also goes out on the same roads, but U-turns and returns and remains in the close vicinity of the temple, where the child is born. The swamis follow. They all stop at homes along the way, where they are tended to, allowed to sit and given refreshment. Eventually, Pecchayiamman returns to the front of the Angalamman temple, where people have been waiting for a fire dance spectacle to commence. That finishes–and then Pecchayiamman’s vahana carries her West, further into the neighborhood.

But Pecchayiamman is Angala Parameswari. She assumes her true form and at some point in this street theatrical performance, the child takes on the form of Shiva’s fearful Bhairava. Together they destroy the fortress and kill the demon king, turning the place into a burial ground.

Here the story intersects with that of Siva carrying the hungry kapala in graveyards–which is apparently one for tomorrow, when Parvati fuses herself to Shiva and they become the Ardhanariswara form, half woman, half man. This is why the fortune teller Thirunangais believe themselves to be this form of Parvati and that Amman speaks through them, though it is unclear if and how this is re-enacted ritually.

notes.title: Mayana Kollai or the night of flying vegetables
notes.occasion: Mayana Kollai or the night of flying vegetables
body: The Sudukaadu or cemetery is a surprisingly happy place. Families are out, together, clearing, cleaning, decorating the burial areas of their families. A man in the cemetery told me (Deepa) about his wife’s 11-year old grave, which appears to be in an unmarked location but he says it’s there that she was buried. Here the ground is prepared by raising a bed a few inches, then sprinkling water, turmeric water, flowers and floral decorations, a small brick smeared with turmeric and kunkumam and placed as a headstone, lamp, incense. Then banana leaves are laid on top and the deceased person’s favorite food is laid on top. I saw idlis, kozhakattai, sundal, kuzhambu on rice, sweets, fruits, even ice creams and custards. We hadn’t known at all that Hindus have burial practices, and they certainly do not predominate. But there are plenty of graves here, including one of a G. Sankaran (Deepa’s father’s name), born in 1901.

A cremation is going on at the beach end of the cemetery. At the other end is the entrance. A “shack” is set up to cover two prone and fearsome mud figures: Vallalaraja and his Queen. They are dead, presumably, which is why this event is taking place in the sudukaadu (“the burning forest”). A large hand impression is on the queen’s belly. People are bringing and piling vegetables at their feet. A sacrificed chicken and a “plate” of offerings is at their heads.

Here the stories of Vallalaraja and his destruction intersect with that other great Puranic tale of Siva cutting off Brahma’s fifth head, and roaming wastelands and cemeteries with a hungry skull to atone for his sin of Brahminicide. Goddess Parvati comes as Angalamman, her fierce and terrible form to match Siva’s own, and prepares a feast. She offers the kapala three handfuls of rice. Two, it consumes, but the third falls deliberately to the ground, to draw the skull there and to create a moment for its destruction. This is why the vegetables are piled on the ground–to represent and recall that third handful.

I have never been to this event, so I ask around about what is to happen, and am told that Angalamman’s chariot is out in procession. When it comes to the cemetery (people are lining up on the roadsides leading there in anticipation), the ther will run over the prone bodies and destroy them. The Mayana Kollai offerings ritually recall the goddess feeding the fierce beings of the cremation ground and serve to feed and pacify the kapala, the goddess and the associated cremation-ground beings.

Angalamman’s arrival is preceded by the arrival of several thirunangai swamis – transgender women dressed as Goddesses. They each carry a theechatti, an earthen pot filled with burning coals; the தீச்சட்டி ஏந்துதல் (theechatti enthuddal) or carrying the fire-pot is an offering and vow to the Goddess (நேர்த்திக்கடன்/ nērttikkaṭaṉ). By now the crowd has thickened considerably, and the family-oriented part of the evening is done. There are people I know in this mix: a maid’s daughter, the carpenter and his family. Young, old, everyone from the neighborhood is here. The fishermen boys see my camera and tell me that I must come for their temple festival in Aadi masam. I take photos of them to send later.

When the chariot finally does arrive, Amman’s hair is long, loose, and flying–wild. The senior Angalamman priest accompanies the chariot. The place is such that the ther cannot overrun the prone bodies–but people do the needful, there are fireworks, and commotion, and vegetables start flying. I’m knocked by an eggplant, and a small murungakkai (drumstick) falls directly into my hands. The catching of the vegetables is auspicious, far more than collecting them from the ground. The whole thing becomes like a mela competition and game. Some are distributed later, but the luck of having one fall into your hands is a blessing from Amman.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil, Brahmotsavam Day 5 Thirukalyanam
body: This is Brahmotsavam day 5 (if you count from the Dhvajarohanam, 6 if you count from the Mrtsangrahanam pujas). Thirukalyanams are elaborate affairs. We get to the Chetty Koyil at 8am, and watch the preparations and the emergence of the utsava murtis. Chandrasekara and his consort are seated on Adhikara Nandi. A deeparadhanai happens. And the deities are carried outside the temple for Gopura Darshanam and Veethi purappadu (street procession around the Chetty Koyil).

Alankaram for the other deities and other preparations begin around 945am, and we are told these will take time. We watch the priests deftly tying kalasa nool or coloured string around the kalasas (alankaram which represents the naadis or nerves of the divinities that will be invoked in these). Why those colours, those strings? What She wants, I do, replies the priest. It is an explanation we have heard before and will hear many times over–refusing one’s own agency, replacing it with that of the Divine.

We go home, and return at 11. The kalyanam follows its usual sequence. Kadir from the Ghousiga Balasubramaniya Swami temple (the “Bhai Koyil”) is in attendance, though we notice this only later in photos. There are men around but the crowd in attendance is largely women. Why do thirukalyanams attract such attention from women? Everyone wants the manja kayar, so there’s a lot of it hung on the arm of the bride. Siva here (Somaskanda really) marries twice, Sati and Parvati are the two consorts. But who precisely they are in the temple’s nomenclature, we’ve yet to find out. Uma and Gnanambal, presumably. We leave after the kalyana sappadu, which is sambar saadam, a sundal preparation, chakkarai pongal, applam…
That evening is a purappadu on a Velli Vrushabham (Silver Vrushabha, or what we popularly call Nandi). Bride and groom out and in a processional reception!

Today is also Rama Navami, was that marked at the Chetty Koyil’s Perumal temple in any way? The main Varadaraja Perumal Koyil marks it with a Thiruveethi purappadu; it’s their Ramar Utsavam Day 9–of course–Navami–but we don’t discover their schedule till later.

notes.title: Discovering the Lada Chinnamman Koyil
body: We’d not appreciated the presence of this temple area so close to home. There’s an inscription outside, with the names of the 5 chettiars who bequeathed the shrine and area to the temple in 1835. Peacocks live here, in the wild areas around the fenced off Keni kulam. Here is where the local rajas (chieftains?) would put shoes on and water their horses. So the temple’s Amman got its name: Lada Chinnamman.

Govindarajan from the Chetty Koyil is the Yadava caretaker along with 2 ladies – I think sisters, one of whom is named Sangamitra. They come to sweep, but at various times daily. The biggest problem here is knowing when anyone will come to open the temple. Passers-by are welcome but this place seems unconcerned with drawing crowds in.

Govindarajan tells of how his family had land near the big chetty temple, and they gave that to the temple and moved to Saaram. He’s happy he can come back and work in the place where he was born and raised. He takes care of this temple and 2 others – Sundara Vinayaka near the old bus stand, and one other, in addition to Chetty Kovl duties as needed.

The “complex” has a main temple to Lada Chinna Amman, who appears to be a Naga goddess–her face form emerges from the body of a hooded serpent. In the ardha mandapa is a mooshika vahana and a spear. Govindarajan couldn’t explain why the mooshika in an Amman temple. On either side of the entrance, stand Sri Vigneswarar and Sri Soundthiravalli as dwarapalakas. Outside in the portico stands Pavadarajan and a balipeetham plus vel.

There’s a large, beautiful peepul tree with small neem beside it, a naga prathishta set of stones (facing east) and a Vinayaka plus 2 rats that seem to have been taken from a temple gopuram adornment somewhere and placed here (facing south).
At the far end is a Jaya Vinayaka Shrine with mooshika vahana at the far end, and a Jaya Veera Anjaneya shrine.
Sangamitra tells us of a tea stall owner nearby who used to claim that the paal abhishekam turns the statue which has a Kalinga Narttana Krishna blue. Same with the Amman whose throat turns blue.

The Kulam is said to have been the jeeva samadhi location of an ascetic who used to come here. Someone else said that if you sit by it, you’ll still hear “Om”. But most cannot stay the evening as there are too many mosquitoes.

Also of Bharatiyar, who may have come here or hidden here (Sangamitra didn’t find this believable until she learned his home is just up the street from here), and of the Mother of Pondicherry's Sri Aurobindo Ashram living somewhere nearby with a view of the place.

Devotees who believe this to be their kula daivam (but we don’t know who these are/ from which community) come here for ear piercings, mottai adikkaradu and other small pujas. They cook pongal or sometimes even meat offerings in the small makeshift stoves at the back.

notes.title: Manakkula Vinayaka – Aandu Vizha Day 1 - Gomaatha Puja in 27 Nakshatrams
notes.occasion: Aandu Vizha Day 1 - Gomaatha Puja in 27 Nakshatrams
body: Yearly celebration of the Kumbhabhishekam. The preparatory pujas for this festival started a day before on March 28 (with the Anugnai, Vigneswara puja, Ganapati homam, moolavar abhishekam) and apparently a dance and music performance.

This morning was a 27 Nakshatra Gomata puja and Utsavar alankaram. 27 cows—each representing one of the 27 Nakshatras —are brought together simultaneously inside or just outside the temple to receive structured prayers, Laksharchana, and sacred offerings. This is a puja to remove planetary obstacles (Nakshatra Doshas) and bring prosperity and peace. Missed it–we are still learning how to find out about each temple’s rituals and coordinate and plan so we can be there always for the right ones, but we’ve not yet grown into this project enough to keep up–so will have to wait for next year to come again and see what photos we can get.

I (Arunaditya) go in the evening around 8pm. There’s bharatnatyam going on, performed by children who will be given certificates for participating there. The priest at the Balamurugan sannathi explains to me what a Kumbhabhishekam is, and in relation to it what an Aandu Vizha is. The patrikai outside reads “Moolamantra Chaturlaksha Japahoma Peruvizha”, a ritual being done to mark it. He asked me to attend the Lakshajapa Homam the next morning.

The way they get to chatur laksha or 4 lakhs is a computation of the number of priests reciting, through a number of puja kalams. Simply 4 kalams, 1 priest each would mean 1 lakh repetitions per priest, and more priests means faster progress. It’s funny to think that this is simply mathematically divided up.

notes.title: Manakkula Vinayaka Aandu Vizha Day 2 – Lakshajapa Homam/ Laksharchanai
notes.occasion: Aandu Vizha Day 2 – Lakshajapa Homam/ Laksharchanai
body: We go to the Lakshajapa Homam at 7am, which is Ekadina Laksharchanai on the patrikai. They chant the Vinayaka Sahasranamam. There are 2 priests chanting on stage, but on the speakers we distinctly hear 3 voices – a mystery to which never found an answer! We are vaguely aware of a calculation that determines the number of repetitions of the japa, but don’t yet know the precise details of it. The Sahasrananam is chanted multiple times throughout the day, by multiple priests, which increases the total to be equal to hundred-thousand repetitions.

notes.title: Kannika Parameswari Koyil Rama Navami Utsavam Day 4
body: Deepa goes to the Vasavi Kannika Parameswari temple for the first time, to wander around and find out about its festival calendars. She finds herself in the midst of the Ramar Utsavam!

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Ramar Utsavam Day 12, Thirukalyanam
body: Thirukalyanam, Thiruveethi Purappadu–but we had not started our formal visits to the Perumal Koyil so we didn’t see this part of the utsavam.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil Brahmotsavam Day 9 Ther Vizha
body: Panguni Utthiram starts this evening, and today is the Chetty Koyil’s ther vizha or rathotsavam. We catch it on return, Vinayaka with damana at his feet, Murugan on his peacock, Somaskanda in the Ther, Chandrasekara on Vrushabha, and Chandikeswara as always bringing up the rear. The procession comes slowly back to the temple, paused along the way by women with archanai plates in their homes. Most of these homes are older ones, charming to my eye, many in need of renovation. But many of these places have turned into businesses, as the Chetty community grows, prospers, reinvents itself, seeks its futures elsewhere. What will happen to these great processions when everything around is a business, nobody comes with an archanai thattu let alone to see, or when God walks by locked storefronts? I ask this question to Aruna Mami, sitting inside, but it doesn’t go over well. “Be positive,” she said simply. I didn’t argue.

notes.title: Kannika Parameswari Koyil, Rama Navami Utsavam Day 5
body: Deepa saw the alankaram and aradhanai of the Rama-Sita-Lakshmana-Hanuman utsava murtis in the morning (having visited once the evening before and sought the permission of the priest to attend the pujas of this Arya Vysya Chetty temple, one of several which are privately run and managed). This was part of the 14-day Ramar Utsavam (Rama Navami and Rama Pattabhisheka Vizha, March 27-April 9). There are 25-30 people present, with the ladies singing the Ramavali and Nama Ramayana. Prasadam is sumptuous with a special serving of buttermilk and panakam. What could the significance of serving these be?

notes.title: Siddhi Vinayaka (Ezhai Vinayaka) Koyil Visit
body: This morning, Arun dropped in to the Siddhi Vinayaka temple on MG Road. The priest tells him he was there for the Manakkula Laksharchanai yesterday. The Vinayaka at this temple is said to be 350 years old, while the plethora of prakara shrines around it have come up later. These include: Murugan, Vishnu, Vaidyanatha Sivalinga, a Nataraja hall, Ayyappan, Hayagriva and some other little ones. The ambience is very cozy. The temple celebrates “all events for all the gods”, says the priest – which is a huge undertaking to say the least. The bull vahana was still out in the corridor from yesterday’s Pradosham ul-purappadu.

notes.title: Manakkula Vinayaka Aandu Vizha Day 3 – Sahasra Shankhabhishekam Preparatory Pujas
notes.occasion: Aandu Vizha Day 3 – Sahasra Shankhabhishekam Preparatory Pujas
body: The patrikai mentions: Vigneswara puja, Vastu Shanti, Mrtsangrahanam, Ankurarpanam, Yaga Salai 1st kala yaga puja, Purnahuti and Deeparadhanai.

7pm – Just as Arun is about to enter the temple, a host of priests emerge with various thattus and a kalasa. Accompanied by thavil and nadaswaram, they move to the sthalavriksham for an aradhanai. It is a surprise to find the sacred tree in a remote corner, tucked behind the thronging shoe-stand.
The host soon goes back into the temple to prepare for the Shankhabhishekam.

712pm – The stage has the usual panca-Vinayakas at the back, with a homa-kundam in the centre. Right behind the homa-kundam, on a platform, are two conches – one beautiful large white conch with a silver-capped tip, and an even larger conch that is entirely covered by a silver kavacham. The other smaller conches are prepared and kept on the right corner of the stage. A small carpet is laid down for the ubhayakara sankalpam in front of the utsava stage. The rest of the crowd is kept behind by barricades. The man sitting for the sankalpam alongside his wife turns out to be the Maintenance Officer of the temple. Holding an orange in one hand and sacred water in the other, the two are made to repeat chants. The sankalpam concludes with the declaration of the Sahasrashankhabhishekam” that is to begin. Simultaneously, there is a puja offered to a mandala on the floor, quite a distance ahead of the ubhayakaras.

730pm – One priest chants various mantras, in sync with which three other priests, sitting cross-legged, offer pushparchanai. For one instance, the flower is held above the head, then touched to the forehead, heart and both knees, followed by mudras and movements, before tossing flowers into the air. These gestures and hand-movements differ for different mantrams and are all fascinating to watch.
743pm – other on-stage preparations ongoing on and around the shankhas. The ritual practice here seems extensive.
The puja can be watched on this livestream

notes.title: Sri Subramania Swami Koyil, Lawspet, the morning after Panguni Utthiram
body: Deepa visited the Lawspet Subramania Swami temple in the morning for Panguni Utthiram. It turns out the Murugar Kalyanam happened last night, because the Utthiram Nakshatram began yesterday and ends later today.

Ramanan Gurukkal from the Mani Mutthumariamman koyil near Kamban Kalairangam/ Nelru Bazaar is there – he is mostly at this temple and goes to the Mani Mutthumariamman shrine on Fridays for the weekly abhishekam. He speaks of the importance of the Vel and the special pujas that can be done here. The golden chariot which was acquired four years ago is taken around for ul-purappadu on Krittikai, but can also be arranged for personal pujas on request. He makes sure I have prasadam (sundal and kesari) and takes me to the Old Vinayakar who sits beside the main Subramania Swami shrine–into which we could go directly and take all the photos we wanted. The Old Vinayaka was of course the first here, before the place became a Murugan shrine

Many women come that day with then-thinai (honey-foxtail millet) maavilakkus, each of which had six dots of kunkumam; this is a traditional offering on all days special to Murugan. Many ladies also offer lamps with panju thiris arranged on betel leaves and so on.
There is a steady stream of devotees, moving effortlessly like flowing water, waiting where they need to and doing what they need without bother.

notes.title: Panguni Utthiram: Chetty Koyil, Brahmotsavam Day 10 Theerthavari
body: It is a full moon (pournami) tonight, so the Chetty Koyil does its Brahmotsavam-associated Theerthavari tody. Not sure why they do it in the sea rather than at kenikulam, or what the specific association of Nataraja is with this culminating cleanse. At any rate, Deepa was in Lawspet, so Arun went for this intense but fulfilling morning.
7am - Procession preparations. Chandrashekhara and Uma murtis are in a palanquin, still inside the utsava murti chambers.

728am - The palanquin is brought and placed outside, while preparations are being made all around. Soon the curtain of Natarajar Sannathi opens and I witness the magic of a Nataraja aradhanai for the first time.

738am - Natarajar and Sivakama Sundari are brought out on shoulders. They process around the temple prakaram, stopping in front of the dhvajastambha to face the sanctum. Completing the ul-purappadu, the divine pair exit the temple towards the temple chariot standing at the entrance, facing north. I was convinced Nataraja would be made to board the ther, because the rite is called the ‘Natarajar Theerthavari after all – I was about to be surprised. Nataraja and Sivakami merely went round the chariot three times, and stood still facing it awhile as though blessing it. The priest dropped incense ash at every wheel and tossed flowers at the chariot, and Nataraja-Sivakami returned to the temple, processing once again around the prakara to get back to their mandapam. Turns out Nataraja only oversees the Natarajar Theerthavari, and does not do the immersion himself as I thought.

Meanwhile Chandrashekhara and Uma are ready and waiting, with a full sized mirror in front of them in the palanquin. A small figure on a small palki has been prepared as well - this is the astramurti/ astradeva.
755am - The astramurti is brought for bali offering at the peethams in front of the dhvajastambha and then taken for an ul-purappadu.

The small astramurti is a very beautiful bronze figure. With all the alankaram on him, his little right hand sticking out makes him look like a Veenadhara Dakshinamurti – though I’d soon enough find out that he is the form of Siva leaning adoringly on Rishabha. He is taken to the yagasalai where another priest performs a yajna. Everything else comes to a standstill. This ends quickly, with an aradhanai for the divine couple within the palanquin, followed by a sprinkling of yaga kalasa water.

810am - The palanquin proceeds to an ul-purappadu, swaying as it follows a dallying zigzag path around the temple. Back in front of the yaga salai the astramurti is placed inside the main palanquin, and another small series of rites follows: aradhanai, yajna ash to the murtis’ foreheads, two priests going around them with puffed rice in hand and one more with a basket of sprouts at the back, ending with the tossing of the puffed rice onto the deities.

838am - The procession leaves for the sea after another small aradhanai. The chariot graced by Nataraja though is left behind, which comes as a shocking surprise. Not everybody follows the procession to the sea immediately since prasadam is served within the temple.

I go after the procession which has the simplest of courses – once on the Ambalathadayar Street, it is a straight path directly to the sea-front, from where it is a short southward to the landmark Gandhi statue where the palanquin gets parked.

917am - After a short tea break followed by a few preparations, the abhishekam is ready to begin. The devotees and ubhayakarars from the temple have joined after their prasadam. The astramurti has been made to wear the bare cloth which is when I realised that it was Siva leaning on Rishabha.

After a beautiful abhishekam, carried by the priest, the astramurti moves to the sea! Balancing on the submerged, mossy rocks, the priest takes a full dip with no firm footing as the waves crash against the jagged shoreline behind him. The basket of sprouts from earlier is also here, and gets a rinse in the sea too.
The astramurti is decorated upon returning and presented another deeparadhanai, which is followed by prasadam.
1011am - There is one final aradhanai as the deities prepare to return to their abode. Fin!
The dhvajavarohanam apparently happened later today. But neither of us could be there to see it.

notes.title: Manakkula Vinayaka Koyil Aandu Vizha Day 4 - Sahasrashankhabhishekam
body: Shankhabhishekam
7am second kalam yaga pujai, Visesha homam Divahuti, Mahapurnahuti, Deeparadhanai,
1030am Yattiradanam, Kalasa purappadu, Moolavar Kalasabhishekam, 1008 Shankhabhishekam and 108 for the Utsavar. Dhoopa-Deepa-Naivedyam, Shodasha Upachara Deepadadhanai.
630pm there’s a dance performance followed by an utsava murti veethi ula. The utsavar was taken around the temple, and on a Veethi Purappadu following that. Livestreamed here.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil, Brahmotsavam Vidaiyatri Day 2 Unjal Utsavam
body: By 645pm we are at Chetty Koyil. Unjal Utsavam preparations going on. We remark that it is a more laid back event than the other days. Seems more ceremonial than ritual. Utsavamurtis are decorated inside, then brought out and taken to the unjal – a makeshift of multiple wooden benches tied together. All the murtis are properly placed, but Ganesha and Chandesha are found to have no space on the unjal. More makeshift solutions ensue, with two little stools tied to the front of these benches to accommodate the lone two.
This adjustment delays the ceremony quite a bit. But the Nadaswaram team doesn’t let the delay drop your spirit!
We also visited the Varadaraja Perumal shrine there. Noticed that Anjaneyar in his side shrine was smeared with butter and fruits!

The unjal swinging began. The atmosphere was that of a wedding reception. Gods brought out to sit and swing swing swing, while the nadaswaram troupe play a concert, uninterrupted by the otherwise necessary crescendos which must accompany an aradhanai. They seemed to play an assortment of popular kritis, nothing very unusual. Priests stood around being photographed–it was as though their work is done, and this ceremony allowed them to sit back a little and be acknowledged.  We leave after watching awhile.

notes.title: Manonmani Koyil on Canteen St., Meeting the family
body: After a few failed tries, we finally met the Iyer at the Manonmani koyil today. A lady who had been at the Manakkular Vinayaka temple was there also, and recognized me from having talked to the shastrigal at the Murugan shrine there. It will be the first of many such inter-temple encounters. A few people stop by, “because it’s Friday” says the priest, including a large man in white with a BJP pin, who steps out from a car with 2 attendants. I think he said he has a cloth shop somewhere in town.

There is a class of struggling priests, as we will soon learn, who are often government employees or former lower-level company workers who perhaps would perform pujas or archaka services at their local functions/ workplace shrines etc. They moonlight in a range of roles, as bus conductors for instance. Their attendance to local shrines is both supplementary income and a hereditary-vocational continuity. They’ve not necessarily received formal training at Pathashalas. One Iyer told us once that you can learn how to do basic alankaram and aradhanais by watching YouTube videos.

The Manonmani theruvu koyil as such is run by a family which lives in a building just across  (originally Malayalee from Mahe, long-settled here) and which has recently, just before we come with our inquiries, lost a son–the man who used to attend to this temple, to a heart attack. He, too, had been a government employee. His mother talks to us and tells us the temple story.

The Manonmani Amman, she says, came from the Senkazhaneer Amman Koyil Kulam (water tank) on Pappammal Koyil Street in Vaithikuppam. No idea how it was there to begin with. A Chettiar who lived nearby (she pointed down Ambaltadayer Madam St) had brought and propitiated it, but then stopped (personal difficulties?) and placed it in the well in the house of a carpenter nearby (also same direction) – as it is the custom to discard holy images and forms in water bodies rather than leaving them unattended/elsewhere.

When the murti resurfaced from the well is when her grandfather’s brother took it, installed it in a small space next to his dwelling (where the temple is now), and began pujas to it. So we know from this that the temple as such is 3 generations old, not 100+ years as some have been claiming. There have been 2 Kumabhisekams done, with the help of a Gurukkal at the Manakkula Vinayakar temple who is an authority and had been something of a guiding figure for them. (Turns out, he was also the officiating Iyer’s classmate also, but they’ve long lost touch).

The temple is now figuring out how to continue its traditions in the absence of the son. Iyers have been called in to fill the gaps, but it’s the grandson who takes over in his father’s shoes. He shows us photos of the Amman alankaras he and his father would do. Now he continues between his studies and exams, with guidance from his mother. We’re asked to return for the Friday evening alankaram which will be done by the boy.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil, Brahmotsavam Vidaiyatri Day 4 Shankhabhishekam
body: Shankhabhishekam from 9 to noon. Very very beautiful the abhishekam of all the utsava murtis. Completion concludes the Brahmotsavam. Got to sit and have a small chat with Venkatesa Gurukkal, while the abhishekam was still being prepared. The Shankhabhishekam done on the main inner lingam was such a strong experience. Induced a very intimate self-giving.
Here is the rough schedule:
919am, Chanting at yaga salai, while Shankhas are made ready inside.
Preparations on vandi, all utsavamurtis loaded and taken to mandapa area. Arranged on elevated benches. Order (left to right):
Ganesha, Murugan + consorts, Somaskanda (with Parvati and baby Skanda), the Astramurti, Chandrasekara with Gauri, Gnanambika + Candikeshvara
935am, Deeparadhanai at Karpaka Vinaayaka shrine at back, to start things off
940am, Nadaswaram team playing, seemingly by themselves.
945am, With venkatesa gurukkal, chatting about how the Shankhabhishekam marks the end of Brahmotsavam and how shankhas bring punyam.
1000am, Mulamurti and Gnanambigai Ambhishekam
1024am, Utsavamurti abhishekam
1051am, Rosewater waiting in kalasa. All paused. Maybe waiting for shankhas?
Plenty of smoke coming from yaga salai
1112am, Yaga salai gathering, chanting, music. Deeparadhanai – preparations for the Kalasa purappadu. Pori poured into a flat basket, held by thalaivar. Pori handed out to devotees.

1120am, Kalasa purappadu. 2 Kalasas from yaga salai loaded onto two priests heads. Pori throwing on them before dhvajastambha. Walking around pradakshina. Music is fabulous. High tempo as pradakshina completes.
1130am, Shankhas brought. Shankhas water filled. Two large shankhas. Rest small.
Meanwhile priests with kalasa go into garbhagrha. For kalasabhishekam.
Now shankhas also taken into garbhagrha. Shankhabhishekam follows. Shankha water being poured on Linga one by one.
Looked like there were two rounds. First 108 shankha water was poured. Next the 108 shankhas were emptied of their flowers and leaves put within.
1147am, Over. Deeparadhanai. Flames brought out. Whole troop moves to gnanambigai shrine. Kalasa water poured. Big shankha water poured. Deeparadhanai.
Kalasa brought out with aradhanai flame. Everybody moving out to utsavamurtis.
Kalasas both brought to utsava murti.
Rusrakha mala on kalatisvara, ornaments on others for swarnabhishekam. Kalasa water abhishekam on all. Deeparadhanai.
1154am, Abhishekam ornaments taken off of utsavamurtis and returned to those who offered them. Kalasa water sprinkled on devotees. Then the Utsavamurtis taken for alankaram behind screen.
1200 noon. I think I'm done. It'll take another hour for alankaram. The waiting! Then a final puja and prasadam will be served.

notes.title: Kannika Parameswari Koyil Rama Navami Utsavam Day 10, Ramar Kalyanam
notes.occasion: Rama Navami Utsavam Day 10, Ramar Kalyanam
body: Rama Navami and Rama Pattabhisheka Vizha, Day 10. After Chetty Koyil Shankhabhishekam, a rapidfire blitz visit to Kannika, where the Kalyanam had been on all morning. The day had consisted of: abhishekam, alankaram, deeparadhanai, wedding procession (around the temple prakaram), exchange of garlands, Sankalpam, Vigneswara puja, Thirukalyana homam, Purnahuti. Thirumangalya danam and Prasadam after noon. Entered, took photos from as many angles as I could, got out.

notes.title: Kannika Parameswari Koyil Rama Navami Utsavam Day 11, Rama Pattabhishekam
notes.occasion: Rama Navami Utsavam Day 11, Rama Pattabhishekam
body: Rama Navami and Rama Pattabhisheka Vizha, Day 11. Sri Sita Rama Pattabhishekam & Iravu kaalam Veethi ula Street festival (we missed the latter, a very silly thing as this temple does not do too many such.)

The event is 10-about 1pm (though we get there at 9 and Arun leaves at 930 or so). The routine pujas to the main deity have been performed and people are having breakfast when we reach–buttermilk, panagam, pongal, sundal.

Two bhattars are there to perform, the main priest acts as helper. The whole attending crowd knows each other, so I stand out very visibly. Nobody seems to mind, but I get asked about my camera, whether I’m Iyer, whether I’m with the media etc. all the time. The ubhayakara are the owner of Ram Silks – he and his brother of Ram Thangamaligai, but I cannot tell who latter is.

The ladies present decorate the crown, and I also see them being asked to prepare flowers or help break up the wood pieces used for the homa along the way–these tasks are not reserved for the priests. Nor are they outsourced to teams of professionals, as we’ll see in other temples.

There is a homa performed and a long period in between when the priest indicates to the nadaswaram players to play specific ragas, as with the dhvajarohanam at the Chetty temple. Mahalakshmi Aunty (the one who teaches Annamayya kirtanas, she shows me her book in Tamil) and a few other ladies also sing. The event has the feel of a simple bhajanai mandapam.

I’ve to rush home, get my half-prepped lunch together for the family, and return. When I come back, Rama’s crown is being carried in a pradakshina around the temple, just in time. Finally the pattabhishekam happens, followed by various pujas and blessings of the crowd assembled. Ram Silks owner gives dakshnina to the 2 priests.

There is a veethi ula in the evening which we do not attend, and that is a stupid lapse, in retrospect as Kannika Parameswari does not have so many street processions. Will have to rectify this in the coming year.

notes.title: Manakkula Vinayaka Moolamantra Chaturlaksha Japahoma Peruvizha or Aandu Vizha Day 5 - Pancha Vinayaka Veethi ula
notes.occasion: Moolamantra Chaturlaksha Japahoma Peruvizha or Aandu Vizha Day 5 - Pancha Vinayaka Veethi ula
body: The japahomam starts in the morning when I am busy at the Kannika Parameswari Ramar Pattabhishekam, and continues through the afternoon. The event is livestreamed here (Britain Tamil Bhakti).
We attend in the evening for the Pancha Murti Vinayaka Veethi ula.

The utsavars are all dressed up, 5 vinayaka forms in all. The vandis are ready outside but everyone is waiting on the ubhayakarar who must be there, and only then the swamis are taken out around the temple prakaram. Timing given is 7pm, but the swamis don’t come out until 9 (gosh, the waiting, the delays), and the procession starts around 930pm (and go up Nehru street, where we follow them, but after that what route?). We go home and return twice in this process. Meantime, the vahana and vandi owners have been around and waiting since 730pm – they’re paid for this work, so they don’t care

Everyone works part time, they have day jobs. The man we speak to works at a school in a maintenance role. We speak for long about the part time gig-work like system all around, as being the only way to make things work – from the priests down to the men arranging the carts for street festivals.
The Gajavahana is from the Chetty koyil, we learn from the man managing them, that he coordinates 40 temples, and they share these resources between them freely. No cost. If a temple asks, they give.

Revathy is the lady manning the shoe stall, she’s from Tirunelveli. Talks to us about the costs of the tenders for the shoe and shop stalls, that people leave chappals outside and she can’t say anything, that the crowds are little so they barely get by. All the temples seem to get by, by giving spaces around them out for rent.

Why did you come here, in spite of all the hardship? We ask her. “Because sitting in front of Him feels good,” she says immediately. “He brought me here and made me sit,” she also says, referring to her passage here from Tirunelveli.

The band guys are all dressed up and have no place to go. There’s to be no band, they say, because one group wants one song and another group wants another song. So there’s a fight, so they will just hold umbrellas today and not play any music. Along with the nadaswaram players is a saxophonist? Or someone holding a western instrument.
Arun: Also not to forget the little live mooshikas at the shoe stall!
Deepa: Right! Eating prasadam bits.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil, Ramar Utsavam Day 20
body: Our introduction to the Varadaraja Perumal Koyil was to find ourselves deep within the Ramar Utsavam, already on-going (it had started on March 19, and would run till April 12). This was already Day 20, almost the end! Ample proof that this work of temple documentation cannot happen by “finishing one temple and then moving to another,” but that all temples need to be followed simultaneously. The methodology we’d need to adopt for this work became clear at this point.

We went at 715pm, directly to a mandapa on Shankardas Chettiar street, two roads from the temple towards the Atithi hotel crossroads. This place was once a nandavanam which has now been paved and built over by the family who bequeathed it to the Perumal temple. There’s a 1919 stone inscription indicating who built it. The family’s home remains next door.

The elderly man whose family made this donation to the temple now lives in Salem, he claimed to be the 7th generation continuing this tradition. You can see the temple gopuram from the entrance to their mandapa area, a special point of happiness and pride. It was amazing to hear how much these lineage traditions are valued, treated as sacred, and upheld generations later.

Normally, utsava murtis from the main temple do not visit peoples’ homes. But this is an exception, which the elders have made arrangements for and the family takes this relationship very seriously. The murtis are brought here, a small puja performed, deeparadhanai, and then koyil prasadam for all present. Then the murtis are taken on a street parade and eventually to the main temple by later in the evening (when Arun went back it was past 10pm, and the saattrumurai was going on at the Kodandarama shrine).

We learned of how the Rama-Sita-Lakshamana-Hanuman figures were found floating in a large thotti or basin on the ocean (she postulated that the idols may have been placed there in Mughal times) and there was some speculation about how such a heavy container and idols could have floated to have been rediscovered and brought to the temple. The thotti sits now at the entrance to the Kodandarama mandapam in the Perumal Koyil.

The Bhattacharya tells us about the structure of the 25 day utsavam: Garbotsavam or the 9 gestational days preceding Navami, which is of course the Janmotsavam, Navami, the day of Rama’s birth. This is followed by Ayodhya Utsavam, on the 3rd day of which is the Thirukalyanam and the 5th day of which is the Pattabhishekam. The event seems to wind to a close when the murtis are brought to this family’s home (this happens thrice in a year: Masi maham, Aadi Pooram, and during the Navami Utsavam).

Later, the Bhattacharya at the moolasthanam tells us of the Narasimhar (now at the back of the Perumal shrine, facing the kulam, west) being the adi-moolar–the deity originally present on the site, before this became a temple dedicated to Varadaraja Perumal. These stories of how temples come into being as this long process of accrual, discovery, recovery, bequeathments and restorations is fascinating and overwhelming at the same time. We need to connect it better in our minds to stories of the emergence of Varadar, too.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil, Ramar Utsavam Day 21
body: 1030am when we get there, and there is a Thirumanjanam going on in the Kodandarama shrine. Done simultaneously to both the utava murtis and the main murtis in the shrine. It’s very beautiful, several have gathered–men inside the enclosure, others sitting on either side outside. The process is the same as we’ve seen elsewhere, except that every time a substance is washed off, there is dhoopam (with dhoopakal), deepam (with kodi vilakku) - thattu vilakku, ie thrice.

One of the security guards helps us understand where photography is permitted (though the contradiction of important people taking photos of the moolasthanams and the practice otherwise being forbidden is evident). Clearly people are aware of the many contradictions that structure the daily functioning of the temple, but they find ways to make peace–by speaking of the importance of true devotion, God’s attention to us all regardless of status etc.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil, Ramar Utsavam Day 22 Vidaiyatri: Theppal Utsavam
notes.occasion: Ramar Utsavam Day 22 Vidaiyatri: Theppal Utsavam
body: Election day in Pondicherry! We’ve been told to come to this utsavam, perhaps because it’s a bit grand and unusual. The more formal parts of the Ramar utsavam over, this is part of the almost-recreational Vidaiyatri.

Perumal (the carpenter who has worked at ours) is there, carrying one of the torches–it takes us a minute to place each other, totally out of context. After that, he comes by to make sure I’m ok periodically, and that I know what is going on.

The deities (dressed with pointy shoes and jaunty headgear, fabrics clearly from the north somewhere) go around the temple prakaram once, stopping at the main shrines along the way and then placed onto the theppal. Deeparadhanai happens, and then they push off. 9 rounds of the pond total, the first with music, the second with vedam chanting, the third with prabandham chanting, and all the remainder with nadaswaram music.

The same players from the Chetty Koyil are here and they do a fine job. They seem to play generally loved and known songs (Dikshitar’s “Akhilandeswari” in Dwijavanthi,  composed at the Jambukeswarar Temple in Thiruvanaikaval, located near Tiruchirappalli (Trichy) as goddess Akhilandeswari is the consort of Jambukeswarar; “Aadu Pambe,” by Pambatti Siddhar (or Pambatti Cittar) in Punnagavarali, played at a few speeds, which I very happily posted on Instagram stories with dancing snake emojis). No specific focus on Ramar paattu at all.

When the Rama comes back from His outing, the group is carried by several men holding the rods on either side, and being egged on by the nadaswaram players in the “performance” of different nadais. They cover the space between the Kodandarama shrine and the Desikar shrine (approx), going back and forth playfully a few times – as though they tease, not wanting the deities to go “home,” taking them out for a little longer and a little longer. Finally they return to the mandapa, and the usual closing aradhanai happens, curtain closes, everyone sits to eat (sundal, kesari, and the best milagu samba saadam ever). Many make cones of the leaves so it’s easier to receive the food. Nobody gets up until the priest calls with permission to rise: Heccherike!
Curtain opens again, but the day is done.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Ramar Utsavam Day 23, Mutthupallakku Thiruveethi Purappadu
notes.occasion: Ramar Utsavam Day 23, Mutthupallakku Thiruveethi Purappadu
body: Another Vidaiyatri event. Reach at about 730pm. The pallakku is out by the gate. The mutthus of the mutthupallakku are now just painted gemstones, not studded. Maybe the serial lights count?

Deeparadhanai followed by the emergence of Rama, regal as ever, from his chamber. Sita and Lakshmana on his sides have mutthus embedded on their necklaces. One round of the temple prakara, and out the gates into the pallakku. Another Deeparadhanai upon mounting followed by a long stay before the temple gates for devotees to seek blessings. This was perhaps the longest pause of the purappadu (though it’s even before the vehicle has purappad[ed]!).
Meanwhile the special Nadaswaram team came from (Kolapakkam, SW Chennai).

They were sublime. Playing at the front of the pallakku while it stood before the temple. Or maybe we can theorise that the pallakku did not move until the Nadaswaram team finished with their piece which had everyone rapt! This was a concert in the street, no bookings or tickets needed.

While this was at the front of the pallakku, another independent bhajanai group appeared at the rear – singing and dancing, and with a vilakku of their own. That was music of an entirely different character and tone. But for the pallaq in between, it would have been discord.

People along the way paid as much respect to the nadaswaram players up front as to the bhajanai group at the back–offering money, seeking blessings and generally approaching them with folded hands. Both groups of artists were very gracious, and acknowledged us and our attentions warmly. The dancing thatha in the bhajanai group called us over for blessings!

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Ramar Utsavam Day 24, Unjal Utsavam
body: Ramar Utsavam penultimate day, Day 24. Arun goes for this. Nadaswaram team already performing as I enter at 730pm. As one enters, to the left of the Dhvavajastambha on the prakara, an entire stage has been set up for them. The bell is also being sounded by the same dedicated gentleman Deepa di and I met the other day. Utsava murtis are in their chamber, behind the drawn curtain.
The unjal utsavam is to happen in the Vasanta Mandapam on the temple’s north east corner, and it is kept lit.

There’s a long queue for the Varadaraja shrine, but as I join and complete my darshan, it seems to be just a regular line, perhaps crowded simply because of the utsavam that is about to begin. I also notice the golden lizards in the ardhamandapa. The circumambulatory path around the garbhagrha is closed on the right. So one can walk past the garbhagrha to the left, but must exit from the opening at the back which faces the Narasimha shrine.

Rama comes out soon, and the procession is very festive. The music is slow and sublime, matched by Rama’s gracious swaying advance. He goes around the temple, pausing multiple times for significant durations, lost in the alai of the music. Upon reaching the ardhamandapa he takes some time behind curtains again as he is raised onto the dais and made comfortable upon the unjal. And once his beloved Anjaneyar is brought to him, the curtains open and we discover Rama in all his reposed glory. A few moments of magic when the electricity goes off periodically, leaving the entire scene lit dimly by the few deepams – there can be no sight more intimately immersive.
Right across Rama, facing him from their dedicated stage, are the Nadaswaram team with their singer, presenting music up to 1am. By the time the priests go home it’s 230am!

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Ramar Utsavam Day 25, Panaka Puja
body: As we enter the temple, there is a private bhajanai group singing before the Pandarinathar shrine. Apparently they gather here every Sunday from 6 to 7, and it’s open for anyone to join. They come from different parts of town, and on Saturdays, they have longer bhajanai sessions at the Pandarinathar shrines close to their respective homes.

Thiruvonam nakshatram today, Perumal’s nakshatram–marks the formal close to the Ramar Utsavam. We go at 7pm. Puja is a simple one, no special alankaram for Rama, simple (gorgeous!) veshti, a few malli malais and a strand of malli tied around his crown – it was the most beautiful. We are told to come back day after tomorrow, April 14 for “Laksha deepam” in the evening – it’s Tamil New year that day.

After the puja we sit (Aruna Mami from Chetty koyil is here and keeps a space for me) and everyone gets a leaf. Panakam comes directly in bare hands only. The rest is a simple Kosambari and a thair saadam which is more rice than curd but delicious.
Monday, April 13 begins 10 days of the Ramanuja utsavam. Not a moment to spare!

notes.title: Chetty Koyil Sunday Bhairava Abhishekam
body: Aruna Mami has wanted us to take her over to the Chetty Koyil for the usual Bhairavar abhishekam that happens there on Sunday evenings. Kodiswarar Sivacharya is there performing the puja to Bhairavar.

Most other temples’ Bhairava pujas happen only on Bhairavashtami, but here he cites some relation (how?) to Sharabeshwara (or Sharabha) pujas done on Sundays in the Thirukanji temple (Villianur) and how that practice came here as a result. A woman reciting the Bhairavashtakam nearby asks why he needs to go as far as Thirukanji when Sharabeshwara pujas happen at a temple in Morattandi – a place which is a Siddhar jeevasamadhi. The connection between that and the Chetty koyil practice isn’t clear. The lady says it’s a time when any Ugra Murti (bhairava, Sarabheswara, Durga/Kali) can be propitiated.
The 4th kalam siva abhishekam is going on. We leave for a glass of coconut milk sharbat at the stall outside, next to the one in which that lady makes those awesome paniyaarams.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil, Understanding the ritual cycle
body: We spend a few hours with the priests (Jayashankar Gurukkal and Sridhar Bhattacharya) of the Chetty Koyil gathering the temple’s practices and annual ritual calendar. It’s a little confusing at moments, partly because we’re learning how the temples keep and time their pujas and utsavams, partly because there is some confusion on what pancha paruvam means in this temple’s practice (there was debate on whether chaturthi gets included in it or not). If the Chetty Koyil follows the model of the Vedapuriswara Koyil, as we soon learn it does, then the Pancha Paruvam are: Maasa pirappu (birth of each new month), Pournami (full moon), Amavasya (new moon), Theirpirai Ashtami (the 8th day of a waning moon), and the monthly Shivaratri (Chaturdashi of the theipirai period, or Krisha paksha).

Ganesan sir asked us to ask about Nityotsavam, but there was no clarity on this. Kotiswarar is new at the Chetty temple, Jaishankar Gurukkal has been there since 2012, Sridhar Bhattacharya at the Perumal temple within the Chetty Koyil complex has been here 20 years, but in no case does there appear to be a very long hereditary line of priests managing either the Sivan or Perumal koyils here. The Perumal Koyil is also relatively new; Kalathiswarar is the truly old deity of this place.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil Varsha Pirappu
body: 830am: We are there for the start of the Tamil new year. It’s heartening to see so many younger folks come all nicely dressed to the temple this morning.

A pancha murti abhishekam happened – Ganesha, Subrahmanya, Sivan, Ambal, Chandikeswara. Most people present appeared to be connected to the Chettiars, they all took big group photos at the end (incl. Aruna mami). There were groups of girls around all dressed up, I wondered if they were Malayali from PU. They didn’t seem part of the Chetty group.

Once the ull-purappadu of Siva and Parvati upon Adhikara nandi was done, we were all sent out and the gopuram doors were shut. Shortly after, they were swung open, revealing to the people (or in our case, re-revealing) the Lord and the Ambal borne by Nandi, through the Gopuram. Perhaps this is the reason to call it “gopura darshanam”?). After Siva was brought out onto the road, puja happened at the Perumal shrine and He was brought out from the temple’s North Entrance (each of the 3 entrances is named for the sannathi most proximate – the South entrance is Gnanambika Amman). Perumal, however, had no such dramatic entry onto the roads.

Perumal was on Garuda Vahana and Sivan on Adhikara Nandi – the combination is special and not to be seen on other days, the nirvagam head Sankaranarayana Chettiar told us. The two vahanas are in part human, part animal forms and both are silver–they “match” in some sense. Siva and Vishnu with their consorts going around the temple on the new year day I suppose is inherently special, two great streams of Indian thought, philosophy and worship traditions.
Prasadam was copious! Kesari (uncolored!), Panchamrutam, a second kesari/ more reddish sweet, pongal, puli saadam and thair saadam. Bottles of water.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Anjaneyar Utsavam, Laksha Deepam
body: Went in the morning, around 1030. Saw preparations for the evening. Stands and trays have been arranged for Deepams to be lit and placed.

44th Anjaneyar Abhishekam for Varsha Pirappu just began. Watched about half of it and left. Remarked that abhishekam items were being used very generously. Apparently this anjaneyar abhishekam tradition began 44 years ago to mimic the same tradition already existing at Thiruvahindrapuram in Cuddalore. A bhaktar used to go there regularly, saw the ceremonial marking and sought to reproduce it here.

We went again at 730pm, the Ramanujar utsavam chanting was about to begin (Deepa got chastised for not having a pottu! It had fallen off. Used kunkumam and looked like mahakali for the rest of the evening). 4 priests sat in front of the Ramanujar shrine and chanted from the Prabandham, closing as always with Periyalvar’s “Pallandu pallandu,” which never fails to move: பல்லாண்டு பல்லாண்டு பல்லாயிரத்தாண்டு பலகோடி நூறாயிரம்

மல்லாண்ட திண்தோள் மணிவண்ணா! உன் சேவடி செவ்வித் திருக்காப். It is not mere closing but a maṅgalāśāsanam, as we will learn—uttering protective blessings for the Lord, expressing the devotee's anxious concern that nothing should befall the Lord's sacred form.

We watched people light lamps and mill around the Anjaneyar shrine which was still active (and he looked super smart in embroidered clothes, set amidst so many colorful flowers), spoke to the lady removing leaves from Tulasi bunches who has been here doing this work for 20 years, she says – people offer tulasi, it gets tied/comes tied in bunches, goes to the sannathis and comes out for her to remove leaves – then is distributed again from the perumal sannathi. Her name is Meenakshi.

notes.title: Ellaiamman Koyil Visit
body: Went in search of the Ellaiamman Koyil off Bussy st. Nearly missed it, because it’s a construction zone now, surrounded largely by Muslim homes. A little surprised by the scope of the expansion, given its location. There are no other major or minor temples in the immediate vicinity.

The priest (Sathish Gurukkal) tells us that this was the temple in Pondicherry before there were any others. He tells of a time when the priests of the other major temples in town, Manakkular Vinayaka, Iswaran and others would come here for the kaappu kattudal before starting their Brahmostavams.

He talks also about the Kamakshi Amman and MutthuMaraiamman deities coming to their “Akka” who is Ellaiamman – processions that would bring them here, and then Ellaiamman goes to drop her sisters back (Kamakshi Amman first and then Mutthumariamman). We start to get an idea of the interconnected processional routes of the various temples in Pondicherry town. Kumabhshekam scheduled for Aadi masam, but the temple seems nowhere near being ready for that.

notes.title: Kamakshi Amman Koyil, Conversation with the priests
body: So of course we ask the priests at the Kamakshi Amman temple about the Ellaiamman connection, and the story becomes a lot more complex fast.

Vedapuriswara, accompanied by Kamakshi amman, would go to Ellaiamman’s temple, and the three deities would then remain at different places in the town – at the end of the Kamakshi amman road (the priest pointed east), near the lighthouse (as far down as the lighthouse/marina), and then what sounded to me like the end of anna Salai near the botanical garden, so that people from each of these locations could come. The trio would stop for a few hours in each place. This festival was once a 3 day affair. It has since shrunk and dried up considerably, owing in part to the destruction of the Vedapuriswara Koyil and to the ban in Dupleix’s time (the priest says) to processions and temple ceremonies.

One room next to the one with Utsava murtis is dedicated to the Balalaya Chithiram or Balalaya Oviyam (etched wooden images of planned temple forms) for the upcoming Kumbhabhishekam. As long as the construction plan is in progress, there will be no Brahmostavam.
The Puducherry Kamakshi Amman is shown standing, and is seen to have a different appearance from the Kanchipuram and Mangadu Kamakshi Ammans (cf. Murugesan’s article on this temple, v1 408)

notes.title: Mutthumariamman Koyil Conversation with Narayanaswamy and Prakash
body: Spent a lovely 45 minutes at Mutthumariamman. Met with a young pusari who is but a boy studying Tamil at the Pondicherry University, and with Prakash who works at the temple, following after his mother who also used to work here. They tell us enthusiastically about the special alankaram done on Aadi Fridays, when the goddess is adorned with velli ornaments. He showed us pictures of the goddess adorned with fruits all around (Thai masam). And also Chithirai Pournami, when she is adorned with all white.

When asked about the Ellai Amman connection, he tells us that there wasn’t any collective veethi ula with all the three ammans together. Instead, three times a year, when Mutthumariamman goes for a veethi ula, she goes upto the ellai (border) of Ellaiamman – this happens till date. They mention the Ezhai Mariamman, Mutthumariamman and Ellai Amman as being a sort of trio. The three veethi ulas are: Masi Maham, Brahmotsavam (Thai Masam), Aandu Vizha (Aavani Masam).

For Masi Maham the amman from Melmalayanur (Angalamman) comes down to Pondicherry. On her way, she stops at a Bala Tripura Sundari temple (the one near Irumbai?). She arrives in Pondy one day prior to Masi Maham, and spends that night at Mutthumariamman temple here. After masi maham theerthavari, she returns to Mutthumariamman, and then she has an Unjal Utsavam the same day or the next, when she leaves for the Vedapuriswara temple. There she has an entire veethi ula with Siva. After this, she heads back to Melmalayanur. On the way back home, drops by Bala Tripura Sundari again and then heads home. These journeys seem as much planned for historical reasons as for practical ones for those accompanying deities on these long travels.

The Mutthumariamman temple has Katavarayan as a protective deity, apart from also having Pavadarayan and his wife (which is unusual, he’s usually not shown as a married man). There is Pecchayiamman, who has an unusually shanta roopam instead of the regular ugra.
There is also an Anjaneyar shrine, unusual for an Amman shrine. But it’s an old one, to which Prathishtha had been done from long before, so it was never removed during the temple’s expansion.

The pusari and Prakash also tell us that this is a kula deivam for many local Tamils who now live in France – there is some evidence for this on the stone inscriptions at the back of the temple. He says also that the Ellaiamman koyil may well be built fast because there’s support for it from those who take it as their kula deivam.

notes.title: Ezhai Mariamman Koyil Visit
body: Morning we go to Ezhai Mariamman down MG Road into Muthialpet, which was mentioned at Mutthumariamman last night, and find it being reconstructed, with the idol tentatively placed in a nearby thatch shack. One of the members of the Nirvagam is there. The Iyer has done abhishekam in the morning and left. He tells us that this is the oldest shrine in Pondicherry (of course!!) and that it is/was a swayambhu murti. He mentioned Sthala Purana or some sort of historical record book that was found behind the goddess, though nothing of where it is now. He also referred to the trio of Ellaiamman, Mutthumariamman, and Ezhaimariamman. Only one veethi ula, during Aadi Masam apart from Masi maham theerthavari.

Mentioned how some of the temple land was illegally sold off by one of the administratives, who eventually committed suicide. It will take another two years for the construction, and the Kumbhabhishekam. We don’t know this temple at all, but feel already the hardships in its way to reconstruction. Perhaps this is why any reconstruction and renovation are treated as processes needing blessings and prayers. So much can go wrong.

Nirvagam member tells us about the iconographic differences of this idol – she has a third eye and fangs, the features of Siva as well as Amman. Three murtis beautifully arranged in the tentative garbhagrha. Stone figure, Bronze figure, and Atti-wood figure [Ficus racemosa, cluster figs of the sort we saw at the Kamakshi Amman Koyil]. Pradosha murti on the side – Siva and Parvati on bull.
The temple is open to all communities. And seems to make sense: Ezhai means poor, destitute. So she is mother of utmost grace and generosity.

Iyers propitiate on all days except Friday when there’s a pusari there all day. I offer something via a QR code on site, and we leave. The nearby shopkeepers tell us that they have been trying to build this temple for some years now.

notes.title: Tales of Two Angalammans
body: Went to the Angalamman Koyil on Chinna Subbaraya street in Pondy town, met Vijayakumar subinspector who told us that on Amavasya Koozh oothara practices are important for Bhadrakali. The utsava murti was out, there had been an unjal utsavam the night before (which was Amavasya). We’re told to come again on Pournami for a similar festival.
We are given koozh and then prasadam is a very nice thair saadam with carrot and mango bits. Somehow manage to carry it all around with us.

I spend some time talking to a woman near the deepam table, where there are small pooshanis halved, filled with ghee she says, and with a kunkumam-smeared red thiri – they’ve used nool, should be panju for better uptake. People who want something leave these lamps – she says in odd numbers but I only see even. 6 Pooshanis, 2 coconuts (she says should be 9 moodis), and 2 limes inverted to make vilakku.

At the Muthialpet Angalamman, there is less crowd. The utsava murti is out here as well, albeit locked behind bars. She is also bedecked because she, too, had an unjal utsavam the night before. Haven’t seen a deity with more arms: four concentric layers! Each extending layer containing more arms than the previous!!
Both temples have “Kalkatta Kali” figures, so named because the pratishtha was done in the ‘Calcutta way’. Not sure what that meant though, and no elaboration was offered.

notes.title: Siddhi Vinayaka Koyil Visit
body: Temple seems so new, but the shrine is 300+ years old. We finally managed to chat the priest up a bit. This was the Ezhai Vinayaka temple, land had been encroached by buildings behind, took them 7-8 years to remove the encroachments, and then to raise funds for the current temple. Kumabhishekam happened last September, presumably at Chaturthi.
The Brahmotsavam is at Chaturthi – dhvajarohanam on Chaturthi, Avarohanam on Pournami.

Temple seems to have a bit of everyone – Ayyappan, Hayagriva, Venkateswara & Garudalvar etc. The Vishnu form was apparently a koshta murti that they did prathishta for, so kept separately. Ayyappan Sabari malai devotees come here in preparation. One lady who was there comes to sing bhajans. They propitiate all the deities there on the appropriate days (Krittikai etc.). Veethi ula only during Brahmotsavam and Masi Maham. All the deities are small, a foot or so, including the Vinayaka who looks like the Manakkular deity, down to the metal ornamentation of his body and beaten brass cladding in his shrine.  Smaller deities have more power, says the priest.

The priest mentioned the fact that the 8 year gap had impaired the flow of devotees – people with flower shops nearby have died, regular devotees go elsewhere now, and there’s a need to drum up interest with a YouTube channel or other social media posts. Used to be a temple for all the poor in the area (at the end of MG road), but has since become the Siddhi Vinayaka temple.

notes.title: Building the Chetty Koyil ritual calendar and Krittikai
notes.occasion: Building the ritual calendar and Krittikai
body: We go to meet the Gurukkal and Nirvagam head at the Chetty Koyil this evening. Much to learn about how ritual calendars are organized and under what circumstances temples continue to function. We take it for granted that the temple gets rental income from its surrounding properties, but these can be uncertain and precarious sources. The Nirvagam head (Shankarnarayana Chettiar) tells us about the Ayira Vysya community whose temple this is. The community’s origin story is one not unlike that of the Arya Vysyas (whose temple Kannika Parameswari is), and will be recorded in our other notes. The similarity of names is striking, but perhaps a coincidence. Both are prominent merchant groups in Pondicherry. The community and its shrine have been around from colonial times, as we know well from entries in Ananda Rangapillai’s diaries (1736 to 1761), and have played no small role in protecting and ensuring the continuity of Hindu practices in the town. Murtis from the destroyed Vedapuriswara temple were brought here for safekeeping, we have often been told.

A unique feature of the Chetty Koyil, as it is commonly known, is that it houses both Siva and Visnu temples in the same complex. Why? Because Chettiars themselves are both Saiva and Vaishnava. (We find something similar at Kannika Parameswari, which pays obeisance to both Rama, Andal etc. as well as deities in the lineage of Siva).
After all our conversations, there is a Murugan abhishekam and ul-purappadu to mark Krittikai, around 730pm - 830pm. Shankaranarayana Chettiar is there unfailingly for every event.

notes.title: Srinivasa Perumal Koyil Visit
body: We’re exploring this temple a little further up MG Road into Muthialpet as a second Perumal shrine to document. This is a Thenkalai temple (the town’s big Perumal temple is Vadakalai). We walk in to 3 weddings in process, thanks Trittiya perhaps (Akshaya Trittiya was yesterday). The Bhattacharya is the same one (of 2) who had performed the Pattabhishekam and Thirukalyanam at the Kannika Parameswari temple; he tells us the younger Bhattacharya is the one permanently here, he has an IT job, but takes care of the temple. We have to come back after 10 days to meet him as he’s busy with a puja at some other Perumal koyil (which one?). Unclear how all this works.
In this temple, you can see Vishnu in 3 forms: Standing as Lord Venkateswara, reclining as Lord Ranganatha, and sitting as Lakshmi Narasimha. Their Brahmotsavam is in Thai masam.

There are 2 priests, a father and son, who are helpful in giving us this information until I ask about the Satyanarayana puja – which they tell me is done by another group – and when I ask how the responsibilities are split – the father quickly says these are needless questions and we can move on because they have no time to answer. A bit strange how a friendly conversation quickly did an about face. We walked out of there a bit stunned and remarking: “What just happened?”
