What we did learn was that this temple is also a Chettiar shrine built by the Pattusali community. Originally there was only the Narasimha swami shrine, facing West with an entrance to the west. The Ranganathar figure at the Pondy museum is from the Ranganathar shrine here (how did it get there?). But the Padmasali community [Nalli Chinnasamy Chetti from this community established Nalli’s] was also involved (how?) and there was a rift between the two, causing the latter to create a bhajanai mandapam just behind which is now a full-fledged Krishna temple. We go there – it’s a simple shrine – and are given thair saadam as prasadam by a lady cooking behind a curtain (very Oz like).

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil’s annual utsavams
body: Revathi’s father Sekar mama sits with us a long while to explain the temple’s utsavam schedule. He introduces us to the temple’s Maṇiyakkarar, who attends to both this and the Sivan Koyil since the two temples are managed by a joint administration with a government-appointed EO (Executive Officer) at the helm. He is very helpful and advises us (in effect) to come in as bhaktas. Everyone takes photos, so what’s to stop us from doing the same, in that capacity. We are also introduced to Rajagopala Thathacharya, who is a goldmine of stories, songs, and insights. He is the one who first tells us that this temple draws its lineage from the Thiruvahindrapuram Perumal temple, which is one of the 108 Divya Desams–this temple is its “abhimana sthalam.”

Atthi Varada figure in the Nirvagam office. Made for the prior kumabhishekam, should have been “released” into a water body, in Saiva temples it’s burned to ash, but here it’s an “adbhutamana” figure and so they’ve kept it with nool malai.

notes.title: Ghousiga Balasubramaniya Swami Koyil Visit
body: We go to Ghousiga Subramaniaswamy shrine around 10. It is a Tuesday, and the temple is packed. The winding queue extends out to the road. We decide to view from outside, and end up getting a good glimpse of Murugan from the East entrance. To the left of the East entrance, is a small Thulasi Mutthumariamman shrine. The shopkeeper woman tells Deepa di that this Amman was submerged in a well that used to be here when she was young. Mohammad Ghouse brought the amman out and installed her there, in a small shrine you once used to need to bend to enter. Only after the temple’s last kumbhabhishekam in 2018 (??), was the room height increased and the Amman shrine becomes what it is now. We see the patrikai for this Amman shrine’s Brahmotsavam, which begins...Ṭomorrow!!

notes.title: Lawspet Murugan Koyil Visit
body: We also make a quick visit to the Lawspet Siva Subramania Swami temple, where Ramanan Gurukkal helps out the main priest (Venkatesan Gurukkal). There is a group of women singing there, led by one Kalyani mami. This temple has an easy laid back atmosphere. Steady stream of devotees, but no special pujas going on at the time we go. Krittikai puja is usually a morning abhishekam to utsavar-Valli-Devasena, and Moolavar and a simple alankaram in the evening followed by deeparadhanai, and a thanga-ther ul-purappadu.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Ramanujar Utsavam Day 10
body: Mangalsasanam, Thirumanjanam, Perumal-Ramanujar ul-purappadu today, as it’s the closing of this Utsavam.

9am Ramanujar is brought out. Prasad given to all is some fine jaggery crumbs mixed with cashews and raisins. Ramamujar does one ul-purappadu round and enters the moolasthana shrine. Garbhagrha door shut. (The security guard who had been friendly at first made much noise while I (Arun) was taking photos.)
At 1030 or so the Thirumanjanam begins.

Starts with sankalpam for the ubhayakara family, who are sitting in the inner prakaram doorway area. When the priests ring bells, the nadaswaram starts outside, in the maha mandapa where we’re all seated. Bhattacharya lights the thattu vilakku and the process starts – milk, curd, fruits, honey, elaneer …

There is sambrani producing lots of smoke, veiling the moola Perumal inside, who is totally bare for the thirumanjanam. In front of the Perumal is his utsava murti with consorts (partially clothed). In front and to the side of this, facing South, is Ramanujar.

Each time the priest shows the dhoop, arati deepam, and then thattu deepam to all the figures. In between each abhishekam step, the deities are washed with water. Perumal utsava murti is garlanded first with tulasi, then with flowers. Such a rich and intense scene. The flames of the deepams and aradhanais visible through the smoke, partially lighting the deities is like some occult dream, shining light on parts of yourself within. It was a very paavam feeling not being able to be inside the sanctum with those performing the abhishekam! There is prabandham chanting for some time.

At the end, the curtain is drawn, we stand up, when it’s opened again, there is another water pouring from the kalasa this time (where was it set before? When was it prepared?), but with the use of a special silver pouring instrument, over a plate [sahasra dhaara/ velli jalladai] crafted so the kalasa theertham will come through in a shower. This kalasa theertha is done for the main deity first and then for the utsava murtis, ending with Ramanujar.
Sekar Mama tells us now alankaram will take an hour, I presume at that time there’s another aradhanai and prasadam distribution.

Evening purappadu starts 7pm – April 22 is the most important day, with Perumal and Ramanuja going out on procession together, “ethir sevai” (Ramanujar always faces Perumal, going backwards white He goes forwards). More like 8pm by the time it begins.

Tomorrow is Punar Poosam nakshatram [Punar Paruvam/ Punarpoosam or Punarvasu] – birth star of Rama, so it’s marked with abhishekam and ul-purappadu – though Prasanna said the abhishekam part wasn’t yet confirmed.

notes.title: Ghousiga Balasubramaniya Swami, Thulasi Mariamman Brahmotsavam Preparatory Pujas
body: 9pm. Arun and I make a “quick” stop, catch the end of the homam which is a small affair done on the street which is blocked for this and by the ther and the mooshika vahana. There are 2 musicians, 1 nadaswaram, 1 thavil. Vastu Shanti happens, with the purusha fashioned in grass and dragged around the temple by one of the usual priests normally inside the temple.

The Vinayaka purappadu also stopped a block away outside an SBI bank where there’s a single stone covered in manjal. Mrtsangrahanam happened here. There a quick altar set up and a body like figure quickly fashioned with some gravel brought on a plate from the temple. Some flowers and words said over this, deeparadhanai for the pillaiyar and the figure was dismantled and the flowers and sand/gravel returned to the plate. The purappadu continued as usual & we headed home.
Tomorrow’s Brahmotsavam starts with the flag raising at 930am.

notes.title: Draupadi Amman Koyil Visit
body: Arun pointed out that this is closer than I had thought, so we stopped by there. A deserted place at first, then a lady and her son came by and told us that their family had been taking care of this temple for 11 generations, the son’s name is Parthiban (works at HCL chennai, the family lives nearby in a joint set up), his father used to attend to the temple, now his Periappa (Rangaradjou) does. Photos are in the entry corridor.

There are two shrines at the back, on the left is newly built but apparently abandoned, on the right is abandoned with a Mariamman kept outside. The left shrine was built in a way that doesn’t allow a kalasa placement so they’ve left it as is. The wall of the right shrine was a part of a border dispute matter that apparently the other party won, so that, too, remains as it is. The Mariamman is a mis-fit in the temple, was brought by a man who had basically discarded it, but honored here by the priest as a parivara devata (or part of the family of dieties in the temple).

There is a small Vinayaka Shrine to the left of Draupadi amman (she is in a garba griha, there is an ardha mandapa, and then an open maha mandapam). To her right, facing south is an utsava murti room – wooden or stucco in the outer area, and brass ones inside, including one of Draupadi herself which Rangaradjou swami says is 1200 years old according to some government department and the pockmarks on the head and face apparently bear testament to its age. The parrot is broken off (another sign of age); “if a parrot then it’s Draupadi”.

Opposite Amman is a small “Por mannan” – the local name given to the “captain” who is really Amman’s brother, Dhrishtadyumna – both were born of fire, to kill Dronacharya. He rises out of the fire fully grown, a crown on his head, bow and sword in his hands. Kunti sits left of him, and Hanuman to the right, facing West, slightly set back in his own shrine.

In the mandapa at the right of the temple as you enter is Parashakti – the sort one finds above the Kalkatta kali in the Angalamman temples. Vahanas “strewn” around, presumably brought out only in Aadi, when the temple has its main Mahotsavam.
Used to be a Dharmaraja koyil, Draupadi amman is frequently worshipped alongside him. The street names attest to this: “Isparin Dharmaradja Covil Street” in Gallicized form, Iswaran Dharmaraja.

The main priest is a lovely, affable man, with many stories related to the myth and lore of the place, with a sprinkling of historical facts about Dupleix having broken the Vedapuriswara Koyil but allowed this one and even bequeathed land near Ginger hotel for their theemitti utsavam in Aadi masam. Some story here about a child having fallen on the neruppu when it was held closer to the “white house” area (he meant white town), the festival being stopped, and then some land bequeathed or permission granted in a ground that is opposite Ginger hotel. They walk from the temple and there and back on that day.

Aadi maasam is when the temple has the most visitors. A full 30+ days, every day something happening and the family makes all the arrangements. They also give tokens for people wanting to come and make pongal here, and Periappa said many times that they get 1200 or so tokens – which is to be multiplied by whatever the cost of each may be. There are indeed many cooking stoves in the back, almost long every wall. The cooking goes on all night, people standing from 1130pm onwards, and the puja next morning happening 530/6am.

notes.title: Ghousiga Balasubramaniya Swami Koyil Thulasi Mariamman Brahmotsavam Day 1, Dhvajarohanam and Chandraprabha
notes.occasion: Thulasi Mariamman Brahmotsavam Day 1, Dhvajarohanam and Chandraprabha
body: We are delayed at the Draupadi amman temple, but get here just at the right time – there’s a different family sponsoring the event and a small group in attendance. The rites are very Vedic and similar to the Chetty Koyil but simpler and shorter. The flag makes a pradakshina around the temple (which means going through the Ghousiga temple and coming out on the east side) and is hoisted. The kaappu is tied for 3 or 4 people.

Prasadam is kesari and chundal. It’s all done by 1130 am. We spend some time talking to a man, who lives a few streets down. He told us this amman was in a well that is still there in the plot just facing/east of the temple itself. Ghouse had a dream about it and had someone get the amman out. He also told us that the Ellaiamman temple was frequented in Rajaraja chola’s time – for the big Villianur Iswaran temple, this was Ellai.
The Murugan moolavar was apparently made by the same shilpi who crafted the Thiruvalluvar in Kanyakumari.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Punarpoosam, Ramar Purappadu
body: We decide to briefly drop by Varadaraja for the Ramar Purappadu (Punar Poosam nakshatram – birth star of Rama). For once we get to observe a purappadu without the burden of trying to document whatever we see (but we do document it nonetheless though, just with some more laidbackness, while being more present in the experience). And oh is it beautiful. So gracious. He’s going to do 3 rounds of the temple. There will be a saattrumurai etc once the rounds are done.

We note just how much commitment and voluntary labour goes into making such a purappadu possible. It’s most often the same devotees, coming time and again to help carry out the procedures. Makes one realise how much personal effort and love goes into making these processions possible.

notes.title: Angalamman Koyil Ritual Calendar with Sriram Gurukkal
body: We sit for an hour or more with the very busy Sriram Gurukkal to understand the annual ritual practices. He is often interrupted by calls and people coming in with work and requests. We often see him in the temple talking to young neighborhood boys who throng about the place. It is just him and the older Gurukkal managing the Angalamman temple. It appears that they function as much as guides and mentors as priests.

notes.title: Kamakshi Amman Koyil Visit
body: This is a Vishwakarma community temple. Neelakantha Gurukkal introduces us to Senthil, the rooster who’s been at the temple for 13 years! We enquire about meeting another day to discuss history in detail. Priest seems happy to do it. He tells us about the pillars of the Gayatri Mandapam and the motifs on them. How each one pertains to a particular story and that sage Agastya placed them where they are when establishing the Mandapam. He also tells us some stories about Marakkanam, misplaced inscriptions during British-era reconstruction of temples (Villinur inscriptions in Bahour), and about this Kamakshi Amman initially being the Ambal at the old Vedapuriswara Koyil which was destroyed.

The priest outside, Natarajan Pusari, a goldsmith by profession, belonging to the Vishwakarma community, responsible for the prakara shrines, performs a Navagrava archanai. Never seen this anywhere else. He seems very dedicated, all his archanais even at other shrines is very thorough, lasting for well over 2 minutes every time. At the Vishwabrahma shrine, he tells us about the Vishwakarma community: black smiths, bronze smiths, woodworkers, shilpis, goldsmiths. The Murugan shrine at the north-west corner of the temple is apparently the oldest shrine here, also brought from the old Vedapuriswara temple. It’s made of pacchai (green) stone. Abhishekam done to it once a year during Panguni Utthiram, and one day before that, he cleans the idol during which one can perceive the green tint of the stone.

On the south-west corner of the temple is a Sakti Vinayakar shrine. Right outside the shrine, on either side of him, are two figures. The one to Vinayaka’s right is a naga-lingam, and to the right is a snake-hooded Amman, with no face. The priest from inside tells us that they represent Rahu and Ketu, the naga brothers.

notes.title: Kannika Parameswari Vasavi Jayanti Veethi Ula
body: Sunday evening. Arun finds the Kannika Parameswari is out on a veethi ula! So we run about and get a few photos – the procession route is long, winding N-S down the main roads and she returns to the temple only around midnight. Kannika Parameswari Jayanti (Vasavi Jayanti) is celebrated annually on the tenth day (Dasami) of the bright fortnight in the Telugu month of Vaisakha

notes.title: Kamakshi Amman Koyil with Natarajan Periyavar
body: Morning at Kamakshi amman temple. Neelakantha Gurukkal points out the fish imagery on the temple ceiling is the way that the Cholas built structures with signs to read to understand seasons changing: when this fish swims up from the south (after spawning), the rainy season comes to an end and the hot season begins. But no idea why these were on the ceiling of a temple. The Cholas used fish symbols to show conquest of Pandya/Chera territory, but not the yin-yang fish symbol that’s there on the outer pillar (near grill), and not the ones on the ceiling.

The Naga knot (naga bandham) I discovered is called a Carric Bend–”a secure, heavy-duty knot primarily used in maritime applications to join two large, stiff ropes or heavy hawsers. It is highly regarded for its strength, inability to jam even under severe load, and ease of untying.” Perhaps this speaks to the Priest’s emphasis on the cholas as ship builders and maritime explorers?

Praveen Mohan has written and spoken about these here. From there I got the name “naga bandham” (resonated from the Thiruppugazh நாக பந்த மயூர நமோநம which of course offers salutations to Murugan as the one who rides a peacock which “knots” the snake at its feet). Indeed, the Kamakshi Amman Koyil’s Murugan sannadhi peacock has the most stunning serpent in the naga bandham I’ve ever seen.

Other symbols (entrance threshold, ceiling near the main aisle): a four-petaled lotus (Chatura-dala Padma) often associated with the physical realm and the four directions. It acts as a "grounding" symbol, representing the stability of the earth and the manifestation of divine energy into the physical world. Maybe connection to Muladhara Chakra 4-petaled lotus symbol, in tantra/yoga. Lord Ganesha is the presiding deity of the Muladhara (root) chakra, this symbol is frequently carved near entrances, on doorframes, or on the ceilings of the Mandapa (pillared hall) to bless the devotee’s entry. Most other temples have just a flower on the threshold entrance, this one seems older.

The rest of the time was spent with Natarajan, who patiently took us around, told us lots of stories, allowed us close contact with everything, and rewarded us with the loveliest manoranjitham flowers from the Dakshinamurti shrine. Such a lovely, affable man. All those in the temple are. And they’ve thoughtfully planted a garden with magizham/bakula, coconut, atthi, nellikaya, hibiscus, kadamba, vembu, vilampazham, and bilvam which is the sthala vrishka. It’s as much a sacred grove as there can be in an urban temple these days.

The temple gives annadanam daily to all who come by and many come just for the food. Even if there’s no ubhayakarar, they give from the temple’s funds after the uchhikalam puja.  Today was tomato rice.

notes.title: Chetty Koyil Rahu Kala Durga Puja
body: 3-430 every Tuesday is a Durgai abhishekam at Chetty Koyil, during Rahu kalam. This is followed at 5 by a Palani Andavar Abhishekam and then of course the Tuesday evening Murugan fete. Naivedyam was milk, panchamrutam, lemon chitrannam, and hot-hot pongal.The navagraha chamber was thrown open during this.
The Palani Andavar Abhishekam was to be done by the new priest, Kotiswarar, and with as many supplies but far less fanfare than for Durgambal.

notes.title: Sri Srinivasa Perumal Koyil, Narasimhar Utsavam–or not.
notes.occasion: Sri Srinivasa Perumal Koyil, Narasimhar Utsavam–or not.
body: Conversation with the priest in the main Perumal sannathi is strange. Old man, never seen him before. Tells us that Narasimha Jayanti is on May 1, gives us patrikai. I ask him politely about whether a different murai is doing the Narasimha puja – “what will you do with that?” he asks me, “Just for my understanding,” I tell him, and he proceeds to give one lecture on how one should keep sights on Perumal and not to the squabbles below (basically). This is the second such about-turn at this temple, confirms my hunch that this is a complex place in the midst of the throes of something and therefore will be risky to try to document.

We are leaving, security guard says “how much did you pay him?” and I’m like “why should you ask that?” so he says “only if you pay him, he would talk this much.” I’m laughing and laughing. Where are the priests? They are not here, says the maid. It all seems quite odd. But the speaker playing the Krishna mantras are lovely.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Narasimha Jayanti Day 1
body: At the main Perumal Koyil, Naresh Bhattacharya whispers thanks for the photos to us. Narasimha Jayanti puja tomorrow 5pm he says. No photos, no video, he says. We nod–it’s a moolasthanam, so of course.

Prasanna is behind a curtain cleaning the Narasimhar shrine & tells us of some pradosham puja today (which Arun never finds), we make our way to the Hanuman shrine where the elderly priest is officiating – he seems chatty, tells us about the connection between the divya desams (Thiruvahindrapuram near Cuddalore and Thirukkoyilur) – Vedanta Desikar came to Thiruvanthipuram & therefore the affinity for him is stronger in this Vadakalai temple.

Ramanan Bhattacharya comes by and is at first wary of us, but when he realizes our questions are really simple and quite benign, things start mercifully to shift. Why does Hanuman wear a betel leaf malai? Answer: Ashoka vanam, Hanuman comes with “good news” so she pulls off a bunch of betel leaves from the kodi growing on the Ashoka tree and blesses him for it – hence this human offering.
He shifts from there to sit on the step near the vasanta mandapam, and we follow and he starts to tell us about the 282 days of utsavams and other events at this temple.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Narasimha Jayanti Day 2, Narasimha Abhishekam
body: 430pm. Narasimha Jayanti – Shukla Chaturdashi of Chithirai. We also read that Swathi is Narasimha’s nakshatram, which falls on May 1 this year. So perhaps tithi takes precedence over nakshatram here. Cleaning and aradhanai of the Narasimha shrine were done yesterday by one bhaktar group for Pradosham (1 murai does it at 530pm, the other at 545pm). Narasimha’s association with Pradosham is interesting – that is the time he appeared to slay Hiranyakashipu which is why his thirumanjanam today is done at this hour. As for the cleaning and aradhanai that happened yesterday on Pradosham day, there seem to be stories connecting Siva and Narasimha – to be read.
The temple doors were closed when we stopped by earlier and we didn’t realize the side door was how everyone was getting in!

Thirumanjanam for Narasimha followed the pattern of all others – the Ubhayakara Sankalpam, followed by the various abhishekam stages — oil, water, milk, curd panchamrutam (fruits crushed & cut followed by honey), elaneer, then a slow application of sandal and turmeric paste which made the murti look like a small kathakali dancer — first sandal on the body, then turmeric + kunkuma used as an embellishment and to add details on the chest, face, and as an encirclement. The water used to dissolve the last of the sandal-turmeric poured on, then water used to wash again though the paste is collected and distributed as prasadam. At each stage, the deity is offered dhoopam, deepam from the ottru kaal vilakku & then the thattu vilakku — especially dhoopam in a specific set of triangular/ 3 point & back-forth movements.

The adhayapakas chanted purusha suktam & other verses & switched at a later stage to a prabandham exchange of sorts, alternating voices and styles. Many ladies in the audience chanted the suktam alongside, and a group gathered after the curtain was drawn to chant again, separately.
After this, the 1st kalam of the Davanotsavam was to begin, Sekar Mama told us. We decided to come back for the next puja kalams the next day.

notes.title: Srinivasa Perumal Koyil Narasimha Jayanti, Thirumanjanam
notes.occasion: Srinivasa Perumal Koyil Narasimha Jayanti, Thirumanjanam
body: Narasimhar Thirumanjanam at Srinivasa Perumal in the morning – a very beautiful darshanam of Narasimhar with the milk flowing on him. “Today is our jayanti celebration, not that of other temples, don’t ask any more questions” says the senior priest who had told us off the other day to someone who enquires. We wanted to see this, so we went, but with no intention of continuing our documentation of this temple, given its apparently contentious priestly and community relations. Didn’t get the greatest feeling from the way the priests were handling people, in any case. If a temple can be a reflection of the unfiltered nature of community life around it, this was a classic instance. We’d only visited a couple of times, and already had a sense of it.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Dhavana Utsavam Day 2
body: We stopped at the Perumal Koyil after, to find a homa kalam for the Davanotsavam on-going. Ramanan bhattacharya was alone in the yagasala, reading verses from a book. Sekar mama had told us (after the Narasimhar abhishekam) that the 1st homam kalam for the puja would start in the evening–we should have returned for it, as that was the formal beginning of this utsavam.

Another priest joins eventually, but there is hardly anyone else around. When he was done, he spoke to us for a little while about the differences between different utsava forms: Brahmotsavam for the well being of the town, Pavitrotsavam for prayaschittam, Damanotsavam for cooling the body of Perumal in this hottest of seasons – each one to create a certain anubhavam/experience and still others to teach, instruct and direct. He spent a lot of time speaking about the “satyam” of different communities – and the practice of measuring paddy in front of Perumal in Srirangam (Nel Alavu or Nel Alavu Sevai) to keep the paddy distributor honest & of the loss of these functions resulting in Brahmins leaving for IT jobs and others claiming the role and function of the barber, washerman etc. I didn’t think this a defence of caste/community divisions as much as an erosion of truths – which the utsavams were meant to reinforce.

But we didn’t press him on the Davanotsavam, which we should have because what, really, is the cooling of Perumal’s body with marikozhunthu (there’s a big pile of it in the yagasala) meant to achieve? But this is also agni nakshatram time and this explanation abounds even in the Angalamman and Mariamman temples, ritually cooling the ugra-forms is not unusual, so we let it be unexplored. Big mistake, as we’ll eventually learn.
Note: Dhavana/ Marikozhunthu is what we all know this Artemesia species as, but in the original Sanskrit it is Damana or Damanam–the word is from the root DAMA or to subdue. More on this later.

notes.title: Kamakshi Amman Koyil Chithirai Pournami
body: The most beautiful Deeparadhanai experience of this morning; rushed here after Perumal Koyil Damanotsavam visit. Not sure what makes it so. The crowd? The manner in which the screen deep within is opened? The absolute stillness there when it is? The flames pointing all in synchoronized lines upwards? Whatever it is, it’s magical. Annadanam and all other aspects supported by one family, doing this for the 5th year. A girl I meet later sends me images of the Ther which was built by the Viswakarma community, and which everyone there has a memory of pulling at night. But because the temple has done a Balayalan in preparation for திருப்பணி / Thiruppani, or renovation, the Rathotsavam is on hold.
There are people selling archanai tickets. The Ubhayakarar family ask what this new thing is – but apparently it’s a government mandate. To raise money! Some people buy. Tickets are 5rs each.
I rushed to Angalamman Koyil to see what was going on – not much at 630pm. No doubt deeparadhanai after.

7-8pm – back at Kamakshi Amman. Similar process to what happened in the morning, including the thundu and food (in dabbas this time) distribution. It was sweltering! Deeparadhanai for Amman, and then for the Utsava murti. I spent long talking to Mageswari who’s uncle is a doctor who maybe is an ubhayakarar for some temple event – and whose ayah lives nearby, so she remembers playing in the temple (and a couple of others around), and never sleeping until they saw the ther on the night when it would be taken out.

notes.title: Mutthumariamman Koyil Unjal Utsavam
body: Unjal at Mutthumariamman – She was in all white, like the moon! Priests weren’t taking colored flowers from devotees, white only. A lady helped me get down and held my head (gently) in place so I could see the deeparadhanai – I let another lady and her clearly mentally disabled daughter go in front of me & a man later sought me out and thanked me for that. Over and over I get the feeling that temples are special for all sorts of things, but among them the collective commitment to aspiring, being better versions of ourselves, generally not worrying about the usual social divisions, being equalized by the focus of the place. But this is not a pre-existing condition, more one that has to be actively cultivated in all these ways. So when people make way for each other in realizing these goals, it doesn’t go unnoticed or unappreciated. I love this part of being in the temple space.

The main priest Jnanavel swami turned off all the lights during deeparadhanai which made it so much more special. He later said that it’s an old practice and “that is aanmeegam!” or “spirituality” which people no longer want – they want to see and feel happy seeing in electric light, so we change with times. There were two pusaris around in addition to Prakash helping out.

Amman’s utsavam form was out on the swing. This temple is known for its elaborate amman alankaram traditions, but mostly in the moolasthanam, where Mariamman is in her full form, seated, and usually very simply but stylishly attired. Dare I call her cute? No, no, no, I dare not.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Davanotsavam Conclusion and Veethi Ula
body: At the conclusion of the Damanotsavam is a veethi ula or street procession. Arun and I watch this a bit together at about 845pm, running from one Chithirai Pournami event to another – 1st time seeing this on Mission st.  So there’s one ul-purappadu before leaving for the streets, and one more upon return, followed by the usual Saattrumurai. There are davanam/damana garlands as part of the alankaram, but nothing outstanding or out of the ordinary.

notes.title: Kannika Parameswari Koyil Chaitra Pournami
body: Caitra Śukla Pūrṇimā or Chithirai Pournami is among the more important full moon events of the year–because it effectively opens the year. It is “rtumukham” or the mouth of the seasons.
ऋतुमुखं वैषा पौर्णमासी संवत्सरस्य, या चैत्री पौर्णमासीति।
says the Mīmāṃsāsūtra of Jaimini (MS 6.5.31)

Also in the Śabara-Bhāṣya, Śābara-bhāṣyam of Jamini, the earliest surviving and most authoritative commentary on the Pūrva-Mīmāṁsā Sūtras/ system of Vedic hermeneutics. (This specific passage is on the timing of the dīkṣā for the Gavāmayana, a year-long sacrificial session. There is a lack of specification (aviśeṣa). When a scriptural injunction mentions a "full moon" without specifying a particular month, the Mīmāṃsā method initially suggests an aniyama (non-restriction), meaning any full moon could theoretically suffice, before specifying Chithirai pournami.

We missed the event at Kannika Parameswari, which we learn about later – but this has nothing to do with Chithirai as the mouth of the seasons. It has more to do with Chitragupta–about whom, the Garuda Purana says:
तत्सर्वं च परिज्ञाय चित्रगुप्तो निवेदयेत् । चित्रगुप्तस्ततः सर्वं कर्म तस्मै वदत्यथ ॥
tat sarvaṃ ca parijñāya citragupto nivedayet | citraguptas tataḥ sarvaṃ karma tasmai vadaty atha ||
“Having ascertained all this, Citragupta reports it; thereafter Citragupta tells him [Yama] all the person's deeds.” (2.18.2)
कृतकर्म लिखत्यसौ/ kṛtakarma likhaty asau/ “He records the deeds that have been done” (2.33.29).

And because Chitragupta records and tells Yama of one’s deeds, this is a day of some reckoning. The Priest tells us about a book which gives the story of Chitragupta, which is bought and handed out on this day. When we go to find it at Giri trading, it’s sold out (we are so amused, as is the priest when we report that to him later).
The Chitragupta Puja here consists of the following:

3:30pm, a “vilakku puja” in which kutthu vilakku (velli deepa sthambam) and a drawing on cloth with a standing figure stands in for Chitra Gupta. The reading of the story of Chitragupta happens directly after and takes an hour. Notebooks, pens are distributed, along with a book of the stories which used to be written by hand and given out in days before xerox.
5pm: the customary Pournami Satyanarayana puja

By 8pm: Chandra bhojanam. All the food is made in the temple madapalli, and they used to eat on the terrace of the neighboring kalyana mandapam when there was no roof there. (Arun’s mother recalls going out and sitting on riverbeds on Chithirai pournami at night, during her growing up days in Tirunelveli).

This mixing of the different meanings of Chithirai pournami is part of what is confusing. The Chitragupta story and its connection to the pournami appear to be strictly speaking homophonic–the names sound alike, but there is properly no connection, except now of course in practice and popular explanation.

In any case there are many pujas we miss on this day, including a Sridevi Ezhai Mariamman theruvu koyil on Perumal Koyil street, doing a 108 Shankhabhishekam (morning), and the vilakku puja at the Lada Amman Koyil/Chetty Koyil.

notes.title: Ghousiga Balasubramaniya Koyil Thulasi Mariamman Brahmotsavam Day 9, Thiruther or Rathotsavam
notes.occasion: Thulasi Mariamman Brahmotsavam Day 9, Thiruther or Rathotsavam
body: We missed this but if the Temple’s rocking Instagram page is any indication, it was a spectacle and a half. Enough for us to know not to miss it next year.

notes.title: Ghousiga Balasubramaniya Koyil Thulasi Mariamman Brahmotsavam Day 10, AM Dhvajavarohanam, PM Unjal Utsavam
notes.occasion: Thulasi Mariamman Brahmotsavam Day 10, AM Dhvajavarohanam, PM Unjal Utsavam
body: We go to the Ghousiga Thulasi Mariamman around 930am. The dhvajam is still up. We are told to return around 1030. We also find out that last night was the thiruther – the ther is still outside with all decorations. Among the decorations are malas of starfruit!

We go home and return around 1040 – and the dhvajam is down already!! We spend some more time inside, receiving pinch after pinch of Kumkum and Vibhuti. Voice-noted the inside prakara walls’ iconography.

Arun goes back in the evening around 8pm. The unjal is already up. Around 830pm the deeparadhanai os done – this is very brief, completed within a couple of minutes. The usual divider-barricade outside the Murugan shrine has been removed to make space to stand before the South-facing unjal. There is a rooster vilakku and a peacock vilakku on either sides of the unjal. To the left of Amman, on a fixed stool, stands Pavadarayan. Amman is beautifully adorned with lotuses, flower garlands, as well as a garland of cloves.

The pusari refuses to let me take photos or videos, although I’d already asked the Ghouse owners. Eventually the elder Ghouse son (I think that’s who he is) convinced the pusari who did not come to me again. I went to the Ghouse son and apologised for any inconvenience and thanked him for intervening.
Met a man who lives nearby. Apparently we missed plenty last night. The thiruther was a big event. He’s shared his footage with me (which is of surprisingly high quality for a mobile).
There is Sundal prasadam.
On my way back, on MG road, I see a ther parked. It comes from the Mariamman koyil on Govindasalai Main road (behind Raja theatre says a man there). This was the penultimate day of the Thiruvizha.

notes.title: Mapping and diversions
body: Morning, Deepa di and I do the theruvu-mapping of the east-west streets of Pondy starting from Perumal Koyil street upto the Needarajapaiyar street. Although we also did St. Therese street (where we find a surprise Atti Ranganathar temple and Ramanujar madam) which is beyond, but we missed Thambu Naicker st and Louis Pragassin st.)
This is the day we stop by Giri Traders in search of the Chitra Gupta stories book the Kannika Parameswari Iyer mentioned – all gone after Chithirai pournami!

It’s a day of miscellaneous conversations. With one of the ladies (attired in blue saris so we know they are appointed temple workers) who hears me singing by the kulam at the back (it’s always remarkable how people in the temple shift agency from themselves to the reigning deity and feel happy to be in his proximity), with one of the younger Bhattacharyas who is usually quiet and reticent, but who advises us to study how Ramanujar and Swami Desikar have “saved” Vaishnavism after the Alwars came and went. He also remarks on the interconnectivity of all the temples–knowing one isn’t enough. This will be a recurring theme, as we’re already finding. He mentions also the position of this temple as Abhimana Sthalam connected to Thirukoilur, Thiruvanthipuram (Thiruvahindrapuram) which are Divya Desams. He spoke again of how the “saving” of Vainavam went hand in hand with the saving of Tamil, of the unity of Vadakalai and Thenkalai in this temple, whereas you don’t see that elsewhere, but he didn’t emphasise it too much as a point of pride.

Spoke at length about how the utsavam practices can vary from place to place according to local realities, cooperation with other temples – eg. Garuda sevai done in some places on the 9th day, but here on the 5th Brahmotsavam day, other adjustments made – but behind closed doors puja practices happening without variation, remaining stable.

notes.title: Draupadi Amman Koyil Visit
body: We spent the morning mapping. A quick stop at Draupadi Amman where we learn of Amman alankaram for Chithirai Pournami and the huge vessel of milk used for abhishekam at the start of agni Nakshatram (May 4, Chithirai 21) – which produced the desired cooling effect as it rained a storm the same night!!

notes.title: Angalamman Koyil Muthialpet Visit
body: Quick visit to Angalamman Koyil to ask about Agni Nakshatram related temple pujas – Sriram Gurukkal mentioned only Agni nivarthi abhishekam with elaneer and placing butter on Amman’s shoulders (? body?), which happens at the end of the 15 day nakshatram period. Agni Nakshatra Dosha Nivarthi refers to the rituals and prayers performed at the end of the 21-25 day Agni Nakshatram (Kathiri Veyil) period to remove inauspiciousness caused by extreme heat and to seek blessings

notes.title: Chetty Koyil Visit, Of Kaalams and Gradations
body: Kotiswarar swami at Chetty Koyil is sometimes just full of interesting insights. We are asking about puja kalams, and he explains them thusly.

He give us this agamic reference which roughly means: ““O Lord, pūjā is threefold: uttama, madhyama, and adhama, distinguished according to the number of principal elements of the pūjā …” ): – in Sivan temples, said Kotiswarar, this is the agama vidhi, how to do puja for Siva, and that follows a series of ritual levels according to the number and elaborateness of the upacaras, offerings, ablutions, etc.
This comes close to this 3-fold “evaluation” in the Kamikagama:
उत्तमं मध्यमं नीचं त्रिविधं स्यान्मदार्चनम् । केवलैः शुद्धशैवोत्थैर्मन्त्रैरुत्तममुच्यते ॥
uttamaṃ madhyamaṃ nīcaṃ trividhaṃ syān mad-arcanaṃ | kevalaiḥ śuddhaśaivotthair mantrair uttamam ucyate || Kamikagama, Uttara-pāda 1, verses 75–76
• Usha Kaala: Dawn / early morning. NA
• Pratah Kaala/ Kalasandhi: Morning, within 10am
• First vilakku
• Abhishekam (no specific order), vastram chaathi, pottu pottu

• Kalasandhi puja naivedyam: sakalaṃ pūrvam ārādhya [having wordhipped everything [prescribed]...], Suryan, Vinayaka, ganapati parameswarasya, Parameswaran, parivararchanangal [all in the parivaram], Parvathi, Bhairava-Bhairavadhvanisandoha (the “mass” of Bhairava’s resonances or sounds, but why mention these)/ Chandikeshwarar, then Bali
• Sangava Kaala/ Upasandhi: Late morning. NA
• Madhyahna/ Ucchi Kalam, mid-day, when the sun (Kathiravan) is at its Zenith
• Abhishekam for Sivan and Parvathi (pradhanam)
• Naivedyam only for Sivan and Parvathi
• No Bali
• Sayam Kaala/ Saya Raksha: Evening (around 6:05pm)
• Abhishekam for Sivan and Parvathi (pradhanam)
• Naivedyam for all, order as above
• Bali
• Ardha Yama: Midnight
• Palliarai purappadu
• Naivedyam for Siva Parvathi only

He then describes the 8 possible puja Kalams as follows; the Tamil explanation is particularly amusing–eg. “0 kalam puja, no worship at all: It’s wrong, and even so it’s wrong” but also indicates leeways, flexibilities, allowances, which are just very forgiving–not how we think of ritual as an almost punitively strict form of worship:
8 kaalam puja: Uttamattil Uttamam (sirappu, aanaalum mika sirappu)
7 kaalam puja: Uttamattil Madhayamam (sirappu, aanaalum paravaalai)
6 kaalam puja: Uttamattil Adhamam (sirappu, irundaalum thappu/lowest/inferior)
5 kaalam puja: Madhyamatthil Uttamam (paravaallai, irundaalum sirappu)
4 kaalam puja: Madhyamatthil Madhyamam (paravaallai, irundaalum paravaallai)
3 kaalam puja: [Madhyamatthil Adhamam (paravaallai, irundaalum thappu/lowest/inferior)]
2 kaalam puja: Adhamatthil Uttamam (thappu/lowest/inferior, irundaalum sirappu)
1 kaalam puja: Adhamatthil Madhyamam (thappu, irundaalum paravallai)
[0 kaalam puja: Adhamatthil Adhamam (thappu, anaalum thappu)]
(I’ve extrapolated 3 and 0, based on the pattern he set).

Siva temples usually run on 4 kaalams, as a compromise and as a way of managing resources. Ritual is a matter of following shastras and accommodating all possible local realities (according to the rule or kalam, according to the substances, according to the circumstances).

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil and Mutthumariamman Koyil Visits
body: We met with Srinivasan Sir (Maniyakarar) and Mannivanan Sir (Manumutthumariamman contact) to get permission and groundrules for work at Siva temple. Sunday is Aandu Vizha for the Siruthonda Nayanar Thiruthonda Sabhai who do Thiruvasagam recitations, all day. They are a separate group we often see at the Nayanmar Sannathi, and at whose request certain specific pujas are done. There will also be a Rudabhishekam, and we get a sense of these two events happening in the same time-place but somewhat at odds.

We also go back to Mutthumariamman, and continue chatting with Prakash and Narayanaswamy. Hear once again about the 10 generations taking care of the temple (in 2 hereditary lines), the importance of alankara traditions in this temple, the “sisters” of this town (Ellaiamman, Mutthumariamman, Ezhaiamman).

notes.title: Chetty Koyil Thiruvonam: Nataraja Abhishekam, Theipirai Ashtami, Thiruvona Deepam
notes.occasion: Thiruvonam: Nataraja Abhishekam, Theipirai Ashtami, Thiruvona Deepam
body: There are 3 events going on, amidst some mutterings and mumblings from the priests
• Chithirai Thiruvonam, Natarajar Abhishekam – along with Naalvar, Pulikaal Muni and Pantanjali. One of 6 annual such events, the most important being Arudra Darshanam
• Theipirai Ashtami, Bhairavar abhishekam

• Thiruvona Deepam or Sravana Deepam – Thiruvonam is Venkateswara’s birth star. There is a small kalasa puja, followed by the lighting of a large ghee lamp and doing one pradakshina around the temple.
Thiruvonam notes:
• Chithirai Thiruvonam marks the birth star (Thiruvonam/Shravana nakshatra) of Lord Vishnu falling in the first month of the Tamil solar calendar
• Shravana/Aavani Thiruvonam is Vamana Jayanti (ONAM)

• Purattasi Thiruvonam is profoundly special for Lord Perumal because it marks the day the Lord manifested on Earth as Lord Venkateswara (Srinivasa) at the Tirumala hills to protect humanity during the Kali Yuga (It’s the last day of the Desikar Utsavam at the big Perumal temple, and day we end up at Thiruvahindrpuram).

notes.title: Angalamman Koyil Theipirai Ashtami, Kalkatta Kali Abhishekam
body: Theipirai Ashtami – 730pm puja for Kalkattha Kali (I suppose in place of Bhairavar as an ugra-form). Arun goes for this. Not a very big event. 20 to 25 members are gathered. It begins at 730, and the abhishekam consists of everything. Turmeric water, fruits, paal, thair, podi, chandanam etc. One unique feature, done right at the end, is of kunkuma archanai for Kali while hymns are recited. This happens right before the Deeparadhanai. While the abhishekam is going on for the moola murti, up above the vimana, the tall stucco figure of Kali undergoes avaharanam, for which she is adorned with flowers, candanam and kumkum. Though the abhishekam and avaharanam begin together, they proceed independently – there is no element of synchronicity. Prasadam given at the end are kesari and puliyotharai.

notes.title: Vedapuriswara Koyil Sirutthonda Nayanar Thirutthonda Sabhai Aandu Vizha & Ekadasha Rudrabhishekam
notes.occasion: Sirutthonda Nayanar Thirutthonda Sabhai Aandu Vizha & Ekadasha Rudrabhishekam
body: Vedapuriswara Koyil has Ekadasha Rudrabhishekam. The Siruthonda Nayanar Sabhai has its Aandu Vizha simultaneously, celebrated in front of the utsava alankara mandapam with recitation of Thiruvasagam all day. Deepa is unable to come.

As I enter around 915am, I’m met with a sea of Iyers. There is a homam in the middle of the mahamandapam, around the Iyers are gathered, chanting. There must be about 35 to 40 of them. I walk to the back and find the bhaktar sabhai aandu vizha thiruvasagam reading going on. Both the homam chants and the thiruvasagam recitations are heard together over the speakers, but they’re not chaotic – there is harmony to it.
I was delightfully surprised to find the two main priests performing the homam to be Saiva scholars at the IFP, Thirukumaran and one other whose name I don’t recall.

The homam has 21 Kalasas near the altar, which are sprinkled with water and flowers. The homam is complete by 1030am and everybody moves towards the garbhagrha. This is the start of the Ekadasha Rudrabhishekam - dedicated to the eleven forms of Rudra: Kapali, Pingala, Bheema, Virupaksha, Vilohita, Shastra, Ajapaad, Ahirbudhnya, Shambhu, Chand, and Bhava.

The abhishekam procedure is unlike anything I’ve seen elsewhere. The accompanying Iyers fill the ardhamandapam, filling the sanctum with the resonances of their chants. The abhishekam ingredients are poured not directly onto the lingam, but through the jaladhara pot which hangs above, allowing a steady flow down. The entire scene has a deliberate slowness to it which, when paired with the sounds of the many voices, charges the atmosphere with an intense concentration. I only got to sit in the mahamandapam, so I really couldn't tell what was being poured. Once the jaladhara was emptied, water from one of the homam kalasas is poured over, followed by a bucket of steaming water. The curtain is briefly drawn then undrawn to reveal the Deeparadhanai – it is always a magical sight behold. After this the next abhishekam ingredient is poured into the jaladhara, and the procedure goes on. This is done 11 times with 11 homam kalasas, depicting the 11 different Rudras getting assimilated into the Formless One.

Minor notes: The lingam does not appear symmetrical – not sure if it has got misshapen due to slow water erosion, or whether it was already naturally so. Apparently after the 11 abhishekams at the lingam, the rest of the kalasas are offered in abhishekam to Amman. I wasn’t there to see them.

notes.title: Kamakshi Amman, Building the Ritual Calendar
body: We sit with Neelakantha Gurukkal today to get the full Kamakshi amman ritual calendar and generally understand from him the practices of the temple. He gives us many insights, and seems especially happy with Arun’s presence as a curious young mind asking questions and learning. Most of what he tells us has gone into our ritual calendar for the temple. Some added detail:
The Meru Sri Chakram was installed in 1978 at the behest of the Kanchi Periyavar

The temple marks a spot on Parvati’s journey – Kamakshi’s penance was done here, here she stands while in Kanchipuram she sits. This is a Vajra shakti peetham, presumably where a piece of Sati’s bone fell (அடி பாகம்/adi, முதுகுப் பாகம்/mudhu). The bones fell in four places: Tiruvottiyur – Tirunindriyur – Tirukkarukavur – Vedapuri.

There is often mention of Krishna’s son - Sambali, praying to the lingam that became therefore Sambalisvarar. But this must be a folk /local interpretation because the term “Samba Koyil” has a different, colonial origin: The Jesuit Church of Notre-Dame de la Conception was also called “Saint-Paul Church,” after the fathers of Saint Paul or Paulists’ first seminary in Goa. “St Paul” soon became “San Paukoil” and then “Samba” in local Tamil colloquialism, and the Church complex, including the Vedapuriswara Koyil, would thereafter be loosely referred to as the “Samba Koyil.” In contemporary use, “Samba Koyil” can refer to the old Vedapuriswara or the Jesuit complex beside it or the current Immaculate Conception Cathedral/ Cathédrale de l'Immaculée-Conception de Pondichéry (which is what the Jesuit Church became)--though the last is the most correct. I learned this also from Geetha Jerome Rajan nee Kondappa, whom I met in Chennai (February 8, 2025); she grew up in Pondicherry and insisted that they had always called the Church “Samba Koyil.”

notes.title: Manakkula Vinayaka Koyil Visit
body: One of the town’s most important shrines, but apparently less utsavam-centric than others? Seems like there are a lot of “pay if you want” options: pulling the golden or silver ther, doing a Muugan abhishekam etc. This temple is the one with the most shops out front. Most others have just women with small tables selling flowers. Here there is a tender system.

The Priest was doing alankaram for the palliyarai murti at about 8:30pm. He never moves out, only Vinayakas Thiru-padam move from there to the main shrine daily. Need to return 9:15pm to see the padam being brought back. In other temples, there is a murti that is taken back and forth (Parvati accompanies on Fridays at Chetty, on Mondays at Vedapuriswara). But here it is His feet.
SANKATAHARA CHATURTHI ABHISHEKAM (4 Times)
• Morning — 6:30 AM & 11:00 AM
• Evening — 4:30 PM & 9:00 PM
On Vinayaka Chaturthi, the temple opens very early, and special abhishekam and kalasabhishekam are performed for both the presiding deity and utsavar, using 21 dravyangal or substances
For Murugan: no special festivals for him except 10 Sashti days including Soorasamharam. On other days it’s only if someone wishes an abhishekam etc.

notes.title: Nandikeswara Koyil Visit
body: Two younger men are the priests: Sivavijay swami and Sivakadhir swami. Some things we learned:

• This temple is the kula-koyil for Dewan Kandappa/Candappa Moudaliar; it is a samadi koyil for Nadu Shanmuga Velayuda Mudaliar [son of Nadu Sidambara Mudaliar, himself a caste chief, agriculturist and interpreter, belonging to the Tondamandala Vellala community, traditionalist and anti-assimilationist, (1845/1846–1908)]
• All pujas here done in Tamil. Priests were trained by a Tamil Scholar at SRM college, Chennai
• Priest also mentions Dr Sankara Devi who speaks on Pradosham days and other occasions on Saivism at the temple’s invitation.
• Kartthikai Thiruvathirai: Manakkula Vinayakar comes here in golden ther now and during Masi maham
• South facing Iswara, like Dakshinamurti
• Siva here is Siddheswarar, Parvati is Siddhewari
• A Youtube video on the temple we found.

notes.title: Nandikeswara Koyil Pradosham
body: Fabulous! There are traditional instruments belonging to the temple, which the players come in to play. They seem just to materialize. They’re then given mariyadai during Maattu pongal. But it’s not just the music, it’s also the priest brothers who seem to move in a distinct harmony with each other, each lamp movement or flower toss done with a certain command, intention, and style. It’s such a pleasure to watch. A lady there tells me that today’s program is shortened because there’s a dance session after, which they just heard about, but otherwise there’s the standard 3 pradakshinas, each accompanied by a different chanting and singing. And dancing!

This music is Kailaya Vathiyam, and these instruments are used only for Pradosham, also perhaps for some other important days. At other times it’s only Nadaswaram and Thavil – with Beri/Murasu only for Vijayadashami. Staying true to its name, the music indeed feels like it is played on the peaks of Mount Kailasa. The instruments used in this Vadhiyam are Udal (the most important, large drums), Thavandai (hourglass-shaped drum carved from a solid block of jackfruit wood or cast in bronze), Sangu or Shankhanadam (Conch), Tharai (a kind of horn), Brahmatalam (large cymbals), Udukkai (the characteristically hollow-sounding drums), Idai vadyam or Thimila (another percussion instrument, almost ghatam sounding, elongated hourglass-shaped), Matthalam (thalatthukku thalaivan! Almost shaped like a mrdangam),  etc. often expanding to 18 musical instruments.
This appears to be the only temple that uses Kailaya vadyam for Pradosham regularly.
We found a YouTube video from November 14, 2024, but with different priests.

notes.title: Nandikeswara Koyil Conversation with Sivakathir
body: Went to Nandikeswara in the morning, met the younger brother of Sivavijay swami, Sivakathir swami – mostly to compliment them on yesterday’s Pradosham. They were trained under a guru in the Tamil Department of the SRM college in Chennai, and have followed his practices faithfully since. It is an all-Tamil koyil with no Sanskrit used. All functions are done in Tamil only.

Also visited the adjacent Gangai Vinayaka Koyil – part of the same temple “complex” though they now are 2 buildings with independent entries and no interconnections. Gangai Vinayaka’s story is based on the story of Ganga being from Agastya Muni’s kamandalam by Vinayaka in the form of a crow. This story is retold by the paintings on the ceiling.

notes.title: Manimutthumariamman Koyil, Friday Abhishekam
body: Friday Masam Pirappu: 12pm: Manimutthumariamman Friday abhishekam. Went to Manimutthumariamman on Chinna Subaraya street, with rain pouring down. Ramanan Gurukkal was delayed because of this but Kasturi Mami showed up diligently. She lives 2 streets down “in a house with a blue no parking sign”. She tells us that this is a deity with powers because all her prayers here have been answered, including the one for her daughter who needed a job and got one. Another gentleman also tells his story being unwell, needing surgery, but miraculously sitting up well again after his grandmother prayed here.

notes.title: Varadaraja Perumal Koyil Friday Thayar Ul-purappadu
body: I went for this in the evening. Simple affair–Thayar brought out in simple alankaram around 5pm, 3 times pradakshina, taken in and placed on the swing (accompanied by Lalli paattu on the nadaswaram: lalli is a type of ritual/ceremonial composition, often played or sung when the deity is being put to rest, especially toward the conclusion of a temple or domestic ceremonial sequence). Sat down for prasadam, and appear to have left my umbrella there. Lost Umbrella Stories #1.

notes.title: Nandikeswara Koyil, The coincidence of amavasya and krittikai
notes.occasion: The coincidence of amavasya and krittikai
body: Amavasya – Nadu Shanmuga Velayutha Mudaliar samadhi puja.
Krittikai – Murugan abhishekam.
Both of these are usually held at 5:30pm, but since Amavasya and Krittikai fall together today, samadhi puja was held at 7am.

We went at 7am, Arun battling a cold, and saw Gangai Vinayakar’s opening jala-abhishekam and alankaram. Then walking round the corner, Sivakadhir Swami opened the Nandikeswara temple. After washing some vessels and bathing the Nandi at the dhvajastambha, he headed downstairs to the chamber directly beneath the garbhagriham and performed the amavasya abhishekam for the small lingam on the samadhi. We realised then that the preponing of the abhishekam meant it got combined with the regular jala-abhishekam rather than being a dedicated event. The only speciality for the occasion was the use of paal in the abhishekam, and a coating of Sambal on the little lingam before it got its alankaram. Coming up, he did the jala-abhishekam for the OM stone and the little Vinayaka before the balipeetham. The moola lingam and Ambal also got a jala-abhishekam. Finally there was a deeparadhanai, first at for the samadhi downstairs, then for the moola murtis.
All deities were then offered naivedyam of shuddhannam and ghee.

We hear from him that initially Nandikeswara was the moola murti of this temple, until the Dharmapuram Adheenam advised them that one cannot keep Pashu (in this case Nandi) without the presence of Pati (Siva). The moola lingam and Ambal were then installed.

notes.title: Nandikeswara Koyil Visit, Bharatanatyam Performance
body: Evening bharatanatyam performance at the Nandikeswara temple. Dewan wanted to introduce us to the man who runs a shop and teaches bharatanaytam (as someone who could help us understand history etc. better) but we had to leave. We end up meeting Vadivelou sir later and seeing him dance at Lalit’s Garden on “Day 0” of the Draupadi Amman temple’s Vizha, some months later. His work and research are on dance forms and motifs. There are amazingly grounded, rooted, well-informed and researched people in all corners of Pondicherry. He runs a footwear shop on MG road close to the temple.

notes.title: Vedapuriswara Koyil Brahmotsavam Preparatory Day 1: Sri Durgambal Puja
notes.occasion: Brahmotsavam Preparatory Day 1: Sri Durgambal Puja
body: VEDAPURISWARA 4:30 PM - Sri Durgambal Puja. This is day 1 of the Brahmotsavam preparatory pujas at Vedapuriswara Koyil.

We are hardly known at this temple, so we’re being cautious, but the elder priest (Gurumama) doing the abhishekam doesn’t seem bothered by our presence with cameras at all. There is a small stone inscription near the Durga shrine which tells us who the ubhayakaras are–the family is in attendance, the lady tells me this was her father-in-law’s bequest. The puja follows the usual motions: kalasa, sankalpam, abhishekam, aradhanai, a group of women sit and sing after this for a long time (presumably they come on all Tuesdays for regular rahu kala Durga abhishekams, and today is no exception) while the priest continues to drop flowers at Durga’s feet. Aradhanai after this.
TAG: Vedapuriswara, Brahmotsavam, Rahu Kala Durga Puja, Abhishekam, Tuesdays

notes.title: Vedapuriswara Koyil Brahmotsavam Preparatory Day 2: Sri Ellaiamman Puja
notes.occasion: Brahmotsavam Preparatory Day 2: Sri Ellaiamman Puja
body: Brahmotsavam preparatory Day #2. We’ve been waiting for this puja, as we’ve been hearing of it ever since the first visit to Ellaiamman–that time when we went in search of one temple, and were led from there, to Mutthumariamman, Kamakshi amman, Ezhai Mariamman and to the big Sivan and Perumal temples in town, all of which are connected to and by Ellaiamman, who was the ellai or border deity for this town. Her temple is marked on early maps–or a “Pagoda” is marked in an area which cannot but reference this shrine.

But the place and presence of this temple in the “network” that is Pondicherry’s ritual life has diminished, and the long Thiruppani or the delayed kumbhabhishekam is not helpful in that–it’s a risky time because such hard-won positions can diminish in prominence or be lost altogether. The Patrikai says 430, but puja doesn’t start till nearly 630 when it’s already getting dark. A man who we will befriend at the Sivan Koyil comes here, and tells us that this puja continues because the family who supported it have bequeathed a property (Rainbow Nagar 3rd cross) or bequeathed the rental income from that property to the temple for this purpose. The elderly lady whose home it was would come herself, but now she is gone and only the money comes. At least that, so the tradition continues. The Perumal Koyil has a similar relationship with Ellaiamman, but they give the money and leave the puja as such (prasadam is delivered to them).

The temple is dark by the time the puja starts. It’s the wooden Balalaya Chithiram image that is propitiated, along with Her bedecked utsavar form. Gurumama comes, along with Ayyappan Swami. Sathis Gurukkal of Ellaiamman is there, the Maniyakarar and the Vedapuriswarar and Perumal Koyils’ EO. All things considered, it’s a simple puja. No Abhishekam as there’s simply no facility for it. Ayyappan swami holds up the screen when it needs to be held up. Deeparadhanai, prasadam viniyogam. Done.
But the large significance of the ordinary in this case is hard to pin down with a single ritual or a few words.

notes.title: Vedapuriswara Koyil Brahmotsavam Preparatory Day 3: Anugnai, Vigneswara Puja and Vastu Shanti
notes.occasion: Brahmotsavam Preparatory Day 3: Anugnai, Vigneswara Puja and Vastu Shanti
body: We happened to be at the Vedapuriswara Koyil this morning, and noticed the ongoing preparations of an all-utsavars-abhishekam. The patrikai did not include this, but we were lucky to be present at the time – or rather exceedingly before time since the delayed ubhayakaras kept everyone waiting, as happens at so many temples all the time. The abhishekam itself though, once it begins, is greatly exciting. The presence of the Somaskandamurti is majestic and vast – one that cannot go un-acknowledged.
At 530pm the Adigu Vinayakar abhishekam was already underway and nearly complete. Arun was unable to come.

The Vinayaka utsavar was brought outside the Vinayaka shrine and dressed up for the evening purappadu. All the other vahanas in dazzling silver were on the other prakaram. A Thiruvasagam group sitting before the Nayanar sannathi continued singing as the Vinayakar puja carried on. It’s Thursday, so Dakshinamurti is also being propitiated nearby. Ayyappan Swami calls me over and gives a mango and a flower from the Murugan sannathi during the sayaraksha naivedyam rounds.

After Vinayaka’s deeparadhanai, the vastu puja begins right in front of the dhvajastambha, conducted by Venkatesa gurukkal who had done the Chetty Brahmotsavam.  He calls two younger sivacharyas over to chant the Brahma suktam, Rudra suktam, and the Vastu gayatri - "Om Vaastunaathaaya Vidmahe, Chaturbhujaaya Dheemah, Tanno Vaastuh Prachodayaat". By the northern entrance, on the floor, is a form of the goddess made in putthu mannu – “anthill-sand”. This is for the Mrtsangrahanam puja. The vastu puja concludes with the burning of the straw vastu effigy, and its dragging for one round around the temple accompanied by thavil on a single, haunting, ominous beat. The man who drags the effigy around is presented with a dhoti before doing so, and is only to step back into the temple after bathing.

Vinayaka meanwhile is ready and arrives at the Mrtsangrahanam site, where a puja happens not unlike the one for Thulasi Mariamman at the smeared stone on the footpath. Numerous shanti mantras are heard, a grid is made with kusha grass with rice in each cadre, and milk is poured and flowers are offered on the manvetti. The manvetti is then used to take some of the earth that forms the goddess figure who is dressed in red. Milk is then poured on the “eaten” body, and the collected earth goes into a Kalavai Satti like thing. It is covered with the same red cloth, now bunched and tied so the tied part sits upright like a figure. A malli garland is wrapped around this red upright cloth knot, and the entire basked of earth is placed at Vinayaka’s feet. The purappadu continues until it reaches the utsavar sannathi in South-West corner.

One of the families whose ubhayam this is runs the Sundara Vinayaka temple (built/ begun in 1910). Rani ma’m, together with her husband and a niece from Chennai are the ones sponsoring this event. Once again, it is this network of temple links that leads us on, and Sundara Vinayaka becomes a temple in our list to document.

Mannivannan comes over, introduces me and Arun to the EO, who seems quite friendly and supportive. We also meet other of his friends who seem social media buffs, and Meenakshi who does accounts in the office. She is to introduce me to Gurumama later. Guru mama I also meet but briefly just before the ubhayakara puja in the main shrine, so he’s a little short. Nothing else noteworthy.

Brahmotsavam Day 1. We reach around 6am. Homam is already underway, kalasas all set up. Some of the Ubhayakaras object to our use of “professional cameras” in the mahamandapam, so we lay off. Rest of the time with no incident. The man from Ellaiamman puja tells us to go upstairs and zoom to take photos. Another who helps carry the vahanas takes me further upstairs for roof level images of the gopuram etc. (he is one of a handful who comes to do the Sripadam work, if that is what it’s called in a Sivan Koyil context, of his own accord).

All the murtis are out and dressed for the event, sitting on tables in the area to the left of the dhvajastambha. The astra murti is on a small stand in front and to the bare left of the dhvajastambha. Eventually this area is cordoned off, so only the priests, players and odhuvars have access.

Once the flag is up, there is a long bali peetham process. At each peetham the priest declares a raagam to be played by the Nadaswaram, and a taalam to be played by the Thavil. These are followed by a few chants seemingly in praise of the deity, and concluded with the odhuvars singing a partial verse. Only then are each of the ashtadigbalis presented rice-balls.

Somaskandar and all the panchamurtis sets out on a veethi purappadu. I have to leave in between as it’s my mother-in-law’s birthday and we’ve to go carry a cake to her. We’ll have to let our photos do the talking until we have time to sit and write full notes about what the Brahmotsavam is and means in Pondicherry. Mornings and evenings are full, and there’s the family and work at home in between. Notes take a back seat.

Brahmotsavam Day 3. Missed the morning, but came for the evening, and what a show it was. Sivan’s bhootavahana demanded Kailaya Vadyam. They don’t enter the temple, but wait outside. And when He emerges–they take over. There were lines of drummers and kombu players with their large curved instruments; it was a nothing short of a spectacle, meant to steal your heart away and make you follow this strange man.
The moment recalls the brahmacharin’s questions to Parvati, whose heart is given to Siva in Kalidasa’s Kumarasambhava (Canto 5, verse 66 onwards):
करेण शंभोर्वलयीकृताहिना
सहिष्यते तत्प्रथमावलम्बनम् ॥ ५.६६ ॥
त्वमेव तावत्परिचिन्तय स्वयं
कदा चिदेते यदि योगमर्हतः ।
वधूदुकूलं कलहंसलक्षणं
गजाजिनं शोणितबिन्दुवर्षि च ॥ ५.६७ ॥
चतुष्कपुष्पप्रकराविकीर्णयोः
परोऽपि को नाम तवानुमन्यते ।
अलक्तकाङ्कानि पदानि पादयोः
विकीर्णकेशासु परेतभूमिषु ॥ ५.६८ ॥
अयुक्तरूपं किमतः परं वद
त्रिनेत्रवक्षः सुलभं तवापि यत् ।
स्तनद्वयेऽस्मिन् हरिचन्दनास्पदे
पदं चिताभस्मरजः करिष्यति ॥ ५.६९ ॥
इयं च तेऽन्या पुरतो विडम्बना
यदूढया वारणराजहार्यया ।
विलोक्य वृद्धोक्षमधिष्ठितं त्वया
महाजनः स्मेरमुखो भविष्यति ॥ ५.७० ॥
द्वयं गतं संप्रति शोचनीयतां
समागमप्रार्थनया पिनाकिनः ।
कला च सा कान्तिमती कलावतस्
त्वमस्य लोकस्य च नेत्रकौमुदी ॥ ५.७१ ॥
वपुर्विरूपाक्षमलक्ष्यजन्मता
दिगम्बरत्वेन निवेदितं वसु ।
वरेषु यद्बालमृगाक्षि मृग्यते
तदस्ति किं व्यस्तमपि त्रिलोचने ॥ ५.७२ ॥
निवर्तयास्मादसदीप्सितान्मनः
क्व तद्विधस्त्वं क्व च पुण्यलक्षणा ।
अपेक्ष्यते साधुजनेन वैदिकी
श्मशानशूलस्य न यूपसत्क्रिया ॥ ५.७३ ॥
How will this hand of yours, with the wedding thread bound upon it, endure the first grasp of Śambhu’s hand, which is encircled by a serpent? (5.66)
Consider for yourself whether these two can ever be joined: the bride’s silken garment marked with the sign of the kalahaṃsa swan, and the elephant hide that showers drops of blood. (5.67)
Who, even an enemy, would approve of your feet—which used to tread upon flowers strewn in the courtyards—leaving marks of red lac upon the cremation grounds where hair is scattered? (5.68)

Tell me, what could be more incongruous than this: that the dust of funeral ashes, so easily obtained from the chest of the Three-Eyed God, will find a place upon these two breasts of yours, the proper seat for yellow sandalwood paste? (5.69)

And this is another mockery awaiting you: when you, who ought to be carried by a lordly elephant, are seen mounted upon an old bull after your marriage, the common folk will look on with mocking smiles. (5.70)

Two things have now become objects of pity through their desire for union with the wielder of the pināka bow: that radiant digit of the moon, and you, who are the moonlight to the eyes of this world. (5.71)

O fawn-eyed one, is there even a single quality sought in a bridegroom to be found in the Three-Eyed God—he whose body is misshapen, whose birth is unknown, and whose wealth is indicated by his nakedness? (5.72)

Turn your mind away from this unworthy desire. Where is one such as he, and where are you, endowed with auspicious marks? The virtuous do not expect the Vedic consecration of a sacrificial post for a stake in a cremation ground (5.73)
To all of which, Parvati answers:
अकिञ्चनः सन्प्रभवः स संपदां
त्रिलोकनाथः पितृसद्मगोचरः ।
स भीमरूपः शिव इत्युदीर्यते
न सन्ति याथार्थ्यविदः पिनाकिनः ॥ ५.७७ ॥

Though possessing nothing, he is the source of all prosperity; the Lord of the three worlds, he frequents the abodes of the ancestors. He is proclaimed as Śiva despite his terrifying form; for there are none who truly know the reality of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
For my part, I cannot tell whether the Kailaya Vadyam outside the Sivan Koyil that day is the disguised Brahmacarin’s posed challenges or Parvati poised responses. Perhaps, both.

The combination today of Guru Peyarchi with Nayanmar Abhishekam and the Thirukalyanam is hectic madness. We decide Arun will stay put at the Sivan temple while I (Deepa) will move to other temples for shorter periods and return. The hope is to catch the essence of everything, but this means timing it all perfectly. And God knows with delays all over, that’s as tricky as it gets. Thank goodness Pondicherry is small though, and the temples are clustered. I catch only a portion of the Nayanmar abhishekam and One of the Othuvars enjoying a rhythmic session with the Thavil player before heading out. I miss the miss the Guru Peyarchi Abhishekam for the Sivan Koyil’s Dakshinamurti and Guru himself, but Arun gets that.

When all the scramble is done, it’s Thirukalyanam today, another ladies’ event! They seem to know when to come, where to sit, what to look for, and what to take away. It’s like a jolly outing! Photos speak for themselves. The event happened in the ardhamandapam, spilling out into the area right of the dhvajastambha.

Saw Ghouse’s son Kadir come pick up some decorations from the Sivan Koyil; he stayed for the Thirukalyanam. Thursday (tomorrow) starts the Vishakam event at the Ghousiga Balasubramaniya Swami temple (Thursday May 27 to Sunday May 30). Friday is the Laksharchanai. Saturday is Murugan’s nakshatra birthday, Sunday is Panchamurti purappadu 7pm

In the evening is the Nayanmar procession, a form of ethir sevai as the Sri Vaishnavas would say, because all face Siva and move backwards in his presence. The procession is led way at front by a group of women presumably from the Nayanmar Sabhai, singing songs. This is quite a stunning procession just because of the numbers, and the uniformity in the variety of Nayanmar forms.

body: ✅07:00 AM: Pallakku - Mohanavatharam/ Nachiyar Thirukolam Appearance Procession | 10:00 AM: Thirumanjanam
✅08:00 PM: Golden Garuda Seva Street Procession

Brahmotsavam Day 5. The Patrikai lists “Mohini avataram” as today’s alankara, but Thathacharya corrects us. Wrong to call it that, he says, it’s more correctly Nachiyar Thirukolam. He pauses on his way home after the morning’s responsibilities, and pauses to talk to us at the end of the street, across from the (independent) Naalvar mandapam that is at the corner. He speaks about a few things, but this is a key point, so here’s the story:

Kurathalvan was one of Ramanuja’s principal disciples in Srirangam; he and his wife Andal had two sons, Parasara Bhatter and Vedhavyasa Bhatter, both named By Ramanuja himself. Both grew into learned and accomplished devotees.

Parasara Bhatter had profound devotion to both Sri Ranganathar (Namperumal) and Ranganayaki Thayar, but a particular affection for Thayar. He trusted her compassion above all else because he regarded her as the mother of the entire universe—one who never abandons her children, overlooks their faults, and continually pleads for them before the Lord.

Curious about Bhatter’s unusual preference for Thayar, Namperumal one day asked him why he was so much more affectionate toward her. Bhatter explained his devotion, and that he therefore could not regard Namperumal as equal to her in this respect. Displeased, Namperumal challenged Bhatter: he too could equal Thayar in appearance and qualities. The following day, he ordered his attendants to bring Ranganayaki’s garments and ornaments and had himself dressed and adorned in the manner of Thayar. He appeared before Bhatter: now would he be the equal of Ranganayaki?

Namperumal was indeed beautiful, and perfectly adorned. But Bhatter pointed to one thing that could not be imitated: the eyes! Namperumal’s eyes could express both anger and compassion, whereas Ranganayaki’s eyes were filled only with motherly love. The Lord might punish a devotee for his faults, Bhatter explained, but Thayar would overlook them, and intercede with Him, asking that those who had surrendered to her be granted Vaikuntha-prapti.

Thus, in the Sri Vaishnava understanding of the story, Nachiyar Thirukolam celebrates not merely the Lord’s assumption of a female appearance, but the unique compassion and intercessory role of Sri/Ranganayaki. Devotees surrender themselves to her, trusting that the Divine Mother will forgive their shortcomings, accept them as her children, and ultimately lead them to service at the lotus feet of Sri Namperumal.
In the Sri Vaishnava tradition therefore, Nachiyar Thirukolam is the preferred terminology. It really has nothing to do with the seduction of Mohini.

For the evening: Ramanan Bhattacharya had told us: the exit from the temple is what is special about the Garuda Sevai. So be there– was the implication. We obeyed! It was a spectacle, modeled after what is seen in places like Kanchipuram, and we understood from there what it meant to take on the ubhayam of an event like this. Priests were up there with Garuda, fanning Perumal seated grandly in Garudasana. The pictures and videos of the evening speak for themselves.

✅09:00 PM: Procession on Golden Elephant Vahanam – with elephant nadai on the streets! He’s a groom today afterall, and so the nadai matches that. “Nadai (Srirangam), Kudai (Kanchipuram), Vadai (Tirupati)”, said Thathacharya! My friend Chandra confirmed the place associations, each one keeping its own speciality, and spoke of how her mother would tell her stories of nadai-kudai azhagu or the beauty of these large umbrellas shading the deities on their way. We awoke to such details at this point. I’ll never look again at one of those kudais in the same way again. They’re magnificent, and not merely accessories, but fully protagonists in this street pageant. The men who serve as the Sri Padam are also animators, they choose to walk in a few different ways to bring to life the deity form that they bear. Today is a wild charging elephant, but a purposeful, fast, direct walk is “Raja nadai,” but of course. This is Brahmotsavam Day 6.

Bhikshatanar Purappadu was also accompanied by the Kailaya vadyam. We met them near the Mutthumariamman Koyil entrance, which had signs for AgniNakshatram elaneer abhishekam. Another steal-your-heart show. Put me in mind of the descriptions of Bhikshatanar as being so lovely, the women of the town come out full of desire to fill his empty bowl–but their hands and bodies have such heat, the rice they wish to give him turns to ash…

Before the evening’s Purappadu, we sat a while to listen to the Odhuvars sing. What they sing: Appar (Thirunavukkarasar) Tevaram (4th Thirumurai, Pathigam 4.062), Thirualavai (Madurai Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple). I take a photo of their phone where an app displays the lyrics which they are following, though they seem to know this by heart anyway. That is what appears as transcription below:
